Test the program by attempting both valid and invalid transactions, verifying that appropriate exceptions are thrown and handled.

# [CHAPTER 6](#toc.xhtml_c06)

# [Input/Output Streams](#toc.xhtml_c06)

# [Introduction](#toc.xhtml_s224a)

This chapter focuses on Java’s Input and Output (I/O) mechanisms, which are critical for implementing data processing in Java applications. It includes how to use Java I/O streams to efficiently read and write data from multiple sources (that is, files, network connections, databases, and more). The importance of understanding how to work with different types of streams cannot be understated; it enables us to handle data in various forms, from basic text and binary data to more complex serialized objects. This chapter explores the key types of streams—byte and character streams—alongside specialized buffered streams for optimized performance. Additionally, the chapter shows how data streams and object streams facilitate structured data handling. Finally, we will explore Java’s try-with-resources construct, which streamlines resource management and helps ensure that system resources are properly closed after use.

By the end of this chapter, you should be able to explain the role and structure of Java I/O Streams, and differentiate between byte and character streams to determine their appropriate use cases. You will learn to utilize **`InputStream`** and **`OutputStream`** classes for byte-oriented data processing, and implement `Reader` and `Writer` classes for character-based data handling. Furthermore, you will enhance data processing performance using buffered streams, manage structured data using data streams, and serialize objects with object streams. Finally, you will be able to safely manage I/O resources with the `try-with-resources` statement, ensuring efficient resource cleanup.

# [Structure](#toc.xhtml_s225a)

In this chapter, the following topics will be covered:

*   Overview of Java I/O Streams
*   Byte Streams
*   Character Streams
*   Buffered Streams for Enhanced Performance
*   Data Streams and Object Streams
*   Managing I/O Resources

# [Overview of Java I/O Streams](#toc.xhtml_s226a)

Input/Output (I/O) can be as simple as reading a field from a file and displaying the value on the screen. **Streams** are more complex and involve a continuous flow of data on which Input/Output operations are conducted. Java provides a robust set of classes that help us efficiently manage the I/O streams of data. When properly managed, we can write code that processes data sequentially, regardless of its source.

Our ability to manage I/O in Java is reliant on streams that allow us to read or write sequentially. There are two primary types of streams: **Byte Streams** to handle binary data; and **Character Streams** that handle data in a human-readable form. It is important to know when to use a byte stream versus a character stream, when working with data management in Java. Byte streams are typically used when handling raw data that does not require encoding interpretation, while character streams handle text-based data, where encoding is a concern.

# [Stream Types](#toc.xhtml_s227a)

In perfect OOP fashion, Java organizes its I/O classes hierarchically to streamline I/O related tasks. The primary abstract classes are **`InputStream`**, **`OutputStream`**, **`Reader`**, and **`Writer`**. These classes provide a framework for specialized subclasses that can implement specific functionalities.

The **`InputStream`** and **`OutputStream`** classes serve as the foundation for all byte-based I/O operations. They form the basis for handling binary data. The **`Reader`** and **`Writer`** classes provide the foundation for all character-based I/O operations. They support any data source where the data can be represented as characters. Character streams handle encoding transparently, making them especially suitable for text data.

The Java I/O stream framework includes a wide array of specialized subclasses that build on these foundational classes. These subclasses include **`FileInputStream`**, **`FileOutputStream`**, **`FileReader`**, and **`FileWriter`**.

# [Stream Operations](#toc.xhtml_s228a)

There are two obvious types of stream operations: Input and Output. Each of these are handled separately, in what is referred to as a unidirectional flow. The **`InputStream`** and **`Reader`** classes can only be used for input operations while the **`OutputStream`** and **`Writer`** classes can only handle output. In Java, we read data one unit at a time; that could be bytes or characters. We employ reading methods such as **`read()`** to process data in a manner appropriate for the stream and/or reader.

Output streams and writers send data to a destination, one unit at a time. Writing methods such as **`write()`**, work with byte arrays, single bytes, or characters. Similar to reading, writing operations generally occur sequentially, adding data to the end of the stream.

# [Buffered Streams](#toc.xhtml_s229a)

Java gives us the opportunity to buffer streams to improve efficiency. The gain in efficiency is due to the reduced number of read and write operations. Both read and write operations can be buffered. The alternative to buffering would require each read and write operation to directly interact with the source or destination. For large data sets and streams, this is a resource intensive approach, making buffering streams a best practice.

In Java, we can use **`BufferedInputStream`**, **`BufferedOutputStream`**, **`BufferedReader`**, **`BufferedWriter`** to buffer streams. This creates an intermediate storage layer (the buffer) to temporarily hold data. This essentially enables batch processing, where multiple bytes or characters can be read or written in a single operation.

# [Data Streams](#toc.xhtml_s230a)

Data streams are a special type of stream, used with reading and writing primitive data types. The **`DataInputStream`** and **`DataOutputStream`** classes extend byte streams and offer methods for handling primitive data types in binary form. This can be especially useful for applications that require precision and binary compatibility.

Data streams enable us to create custom data formats, often used in networking and database applications, where data type fidelity is critical.

# [Serialization](#toc.xhtml_s231a)

Java’s **`ObjectInputStream`** and **`ObjectOutputStream`** classes enable object serialization. This is a process that converts Java objects into a byte stream for storage or transmission. Object serialization can be useful in applications that require complex data structures to be saved or transferred. An example is with saving application states or transmitting objects over a network.

To serialize an object, its class must implement the **`Serializable`** interface. This earmarks the class as safe for serialization and allows the object to be reconstructed from the byte stream. Object streams extend the capabilities of data streams by handling complex objects, rather than just primitive data types.

# [Managing Resources](#toc.xhtml_s232a)

We can use Java’s **`try-with-resources`** statement to automate resource handling. Resources such as files, network sockets, and database connections typically need to be explicitly closed after use to avoid resource leaks. The **`try-with-resources`** statement simplifies this by automatically closing resources at the end of the statement.

The use of **`try-with-resources`** enhances resource management in Java. Not only will this ensure that each resource is closed after it is no longer needed, it even works if an exception occurs. This reduces code complexity and helps prevent memory leaks.

# [Byte Streams](#toc.xhtml_s233a)

A **byte stream** is how we handle raw, unprocessed data, one byte at a time. They are key to our ability to process and handle binary data in Java, especially when dealing with network data, images, and other binary content. Byte streams are generally efficient because they operate at the byte level without the need for character interpretation or encoding. A common use case is for instances where direct byte manipulation is required to preserve every byte without modification.

There are three types of byte streams in relation to the data source (for reading) or target (for writing):

*   File-based input/output
*   Memory-based input/output
*   Network-based input/output

Byte streams are unidirectional which means any given stream object can handle input or output, but not both. This is not a Java limitation; rather, it allows us to simplify our code, making it more readable and maintainable.

Java’s java.io package contains the **`InputStream`** and **`OutputStream`** abstract classes that define methods for reading from and writing to byte-based sources and targets. Java also has several byte stream classes to handle specific sources, such as arrays and files. This gives us great flexibility, allowing us to use specialized tools for each input/output task. Let us look at each of these abstract classes in the sections that follow.

# [Input Stream](#toc.xhtml_s234a)

The following selected methods are part of the **`InputStream`** class:

*   **`read()`**: This method reads the next byte of data from the input stream. It has multiple forms:
    *   **`int read()`**: This method reads the next byte from the stream and returns an integer between 0 and 255. When the end of stream is reached, this method returns **`-1`**.
    *   **`int read(byte[ ] b)`**: This method is used to read up to **`b.length`** bytes of data into an array. The method returns the number of bytes read. We can use this method for reading chunks of data.
    *   **`int read(byte[ ] b, int off, int len)`**: This method gives us greater fidelity in what we read. We can read up to **`len`** bytes into a specific portion of the array by using **`off`** as the offset.
*   **`skip()`**: This method, when written as **`long skip(long n)`** will skip over **`n`** bytes in the stream. This is useful when we are performing **seek** operations.
*   **`close()`**: This method has the **`void`** return type. It simply closes the input stream. This is an important part of input stream management. We want to release system resources associated with the input stream when we are done with it.

# [Output Stream](#toc.xhtml_s235a)

The following selected methods are part of the **`OutputStream`** class:

*   **`write()`**: This method writes a single byte of data to the output stream. It has multiple forms:
    *   **`void write(int b)`**: This method writes the eight-lowest bits of a byte to the output stream.
    *   **`void write(byte[ ] b)`**: This method writes the entire byte array to the output stream. This is commonly used when processing data in bulk for output.
    *   **`void write(byte[ ] b, int off, int len)`**: This method writes **`len`** bytes to a specific portion of the array by using **`off`** as the offset.
*   **`flush()`**: This method has the **`void`** return type. It is used to push buffered bytes to the output stream. This is commonly used in network applications.
*   **`close()`**: This method has the **`void`** return type. It simply closes the output stream. Just as with input streams, we want to release system resources associated with the output stream when we are done with it.

# [Code Example](#toc.xhtml_s236a)

Byte streams are commonly used in network programming, where raw data is transmitted over socket connections. The following example demonstrates how data can be sent and received using a socket connection:

`import java.io.IOException;`

`import java.io.InputStream;`

`import java.io.OutputStream;`

`import java.net.Socket;`

`public class NetworkExample {`

`public static void main(String[] args) {`

`try (Socket socket = new Socket("localhost", 8080);`

`OutputStream output = socket.getOutputStream();`

`InputStream input = socket.getInputStream()) {`

`output.write("Hello Local Server".getBytes());`

`int responseByte;`

`while ((responseByte = input.read()) != -1) {`

`System.out.print((char) responseByte);`

`}`

`} catch (IOException e) {`

`System.out.println("Network error encountered: " + e.getMessage());`

`}`

`}`

`}`

This network programming example starts by opening a socket connection to a service, it then sends a raw byte message, and finally reads the server’s response one byte at a time. This is an example of a byte stream being used for a low-level communication. Every byte is important, especially when dealing with network protocols.

# [Character Streams](#toc.xhtml_s237a)

**Character streams** handle text in a similar manner to how byte streams work. They have separate input and output streams that process a character instead of a raw byte. Character streams are often used when working with human-readable data, regardless of source (for reading) or target (for writing). In Java, character streams manage character encoding automatically. This allows us to write programs that read and write data as characters rather than bytes.

Java gives us a **`Reader`** and a **`Writer`** class in the **`java.io`** package to implement character strings. These streams have three primary types: file-based, memory-based, and network-based. Let us take a look at what we can do with the **`Reader`** and a **`Writer`** classes.

# [Reader Class](#toc.xhtml_s238a)

The **`Reader`** class is an abstract class that represents a character input stream. Here are some key methods in that class. You will notice some close parallels with the **`InputStream`** class used for byte streams.

*   **`int read()`**: This method reads a single character from the input stream and returns that character’s integer representation. When the input stream’s end is encountered, **`-1`** is returned.
*   **`int read(char[ ] charBuf)`**: This method reads characters into an array and returns the number of characters read. We typically use this method for reading multiple characters at once.
*   **`int read(char[ ] charBuf, int off, int len)`**: With this method, we can read up to **`len`** characters into a specific section of our array, starting at the **`off`** offset.
*   **`boolean ready()`**: This method determines if the input stream is ready for read operations.
*   **`void close()`**: This method closes the reader and frees up any related system resources.

# [Writer Class](#toc.xhtml_s239a)

The **`Writer`** class is an abstract class that represents a character output stream. Here are some key methods in that class. You will notice some close parallels with the **`OutputStream`** class used for byte streams.

*   **`void write(int c)`**: This method writes a single character to the output stream and returns that character’s integer representation.
*   **`void write(char[ ] charBuf)`**: This method writes the entire character array to the output stream.
*   **`void write(char[ ] charBuf, int off, int len)`**: With this method, we can write **`len`** characters from a specific section of our array, starting at the **`off`** offset.
*   **`void write(String str)`**`:` This method writes a string to the output stream. This is a powerful method as it allows us to write text without having to manually covert it to a character array.
*   **`void flush()`**: This method forces all buffered output to be written to the target.
*   **`void close()`**: This method closes the writer and frees up any related system resources.

# [Code Example](#toc.xhtml_s240a)

Character streams are great for working with text files. Here is an example implementation of character input streams and output streams:

`import java.io.FileReader;`

`import java.io.FileWriter;`

`import java.io.IOException;`

`public class TextFileExample {`

`public static void main(String[] args) {`

`try (FileReader reader = new FileReader("myInput.txt");`

`FileWriter writer = new FileWriter("myOutput.txt")) {`

`int character;`

`while ((character = reader.read()) != -1) {`

`writer.write(character);`

`}`

`} catch (IOException e) {`

`System.out.println("I/O error: " + e.getMessage());`

`}`

`}`

`}`

The preceding program creates a **`FileReader`** to read a pre-existing text file’s contents, one character at a time. A **`FileWriter`** is created to output the characters to a new file. For larger files, we would use buffered streams. Those are covered in the next section.

# [Buffered Streams for Enhanced Performance](#toc.xhtml_s241a)

Byte streams and character streams are highly functional approaches to handling byte and character data. However, they can be inefficient especially with large datasets. Fortunately, Java gives us the ability to buffer our streams, both input and output. Efficiency is gained by reducing the number of input and output operations.

**Buffered streams**, just line byte streams and character streams, are part of Java’s **`java.io`** package. The self-descriptive classes we can use are **`BufferedInputStream`**, **`BufferedOutputStream`**, **`BufferedReader`**, and **`BufferedWriter`**. So, there are buffered classes for input and output byte streams as well as a set for character streams.

Buffered streams work by using temporary storage (the buffer) as a staging area before data is processed. We have the ability to define the size of our buffers and that is highly dependent on the nature of the application, the data set, and underlying processing power. This approach to streams reduces the input and output overhead thereby increasing performance, and makes our code more streamlined, readable, and maintainable. Here are some recommendations regarding buffer size:

*   Java’s default buffer size of 8 KB is usually sufficient for most applications. So, try using the default and increase it if you need to obtain better performance.
*   Typically, increasing the buffer size results in fewer input/output operations and greater performance.
*   If your system has memory constraints, consider reducing the buffer size.
*   When working with network streams, larger buffers can decrease latency, improving overall throughput. If you are on a high-speed network, take advantage of it.

# [Code Example](#toc.xhtml_s242a)

This section demonstrates how to use the **`BufferedReader`** and **`BufferedWriter`** classes, which offer performance enhancements over the **`Reader`** and **`Writer`** classes. The buffered approach is especially useful when processing text files and large datasets of character-based data. Here is the example code:

`import java.io.BufferedReader;`

`import java.io.BufferedWriter;`

`import java.io.FileReader;`

`import java.io.FileWriter;`

`import java.io.IOException;`

`public class BufferExample {`

`public static void main(String[] args) {`

`try (BufferedReader reader = new BufferedReader(new FileReader("mySource.txt"));`

`BufferedWriter writer = new BufferedWriter(new FileWriter("myDestination.txt"))) {`

`String line;`

`while ((line = reader.readLine()) != null) {`

`writer.write(line);`

`writer.newLine();`

`}`

`} catch (IOException e) {`

`System.out.println("I/O error: " + e.getMessage());`

`}`

`}`

`}`

In this example, we read and write text data using the **`BufferedReader`** and **`BufferedWriter`** classes. **`BufferedReader`** reads lines from the **`mySource.txt`** source file and **`BufferedWriter`** writes them to the **`myDestination.txt`** target file. **`BufferedWriter`** includes a **`newLine()`** method that handles line separators. The **`newLine()`** method is platform-specific making our code portable. We gain efficiency with this approach based on the reduced number of input and output operations.

# [Flushing Your Buffer](#toc.xhtml_s243a)

It is important that we explicitly flush our buffered output streams to ensure all data from the buffer is written to the destination. We use the **`flush()`** method to force all data in the buffer to be immediately written. Here are some scenarios when this might be necessary:

*   In network applications, it is important to flush buffers, even when they are not full, so messages and data can be transmitted immediately.
*   Real-time applications such as logging and alert systems require that data be output immediately, necessitating the need for the flush operation.

The following code snippet demonstrates how this could be implemented:

`try (BufferedWriter writer = new BufferedWriter(new FileWriter("myOutput.txt"))) {`

`writer.write("Demo: Buffered stream example with flush.");`

`writer.flush();`

`} catch (IOException e) {`

`System.out.println("I/O error: " + e.getMessage());`

`}`

This example demonstrates how the **`flush()`** method is used to immediately send anything in the buffer to the **`myOutput.txt`** destination. This happens immediately after the write operation.

# [Data Streams and Object Streams](#toc.xhtml_s244a)

So far, we have characterized input and output streams by their direction; inward for reading operations and outward for writing operations. Streams can also be characterized by the type of data they contain. **Data streams** are those that handle the input and output flows of primitive data types, such as integers and characters as well as arrays of those data types. **Object streams** handle the flow (input and output) of objects. With object streams, we serialize objects into a byte stream and reconstruct the object to its original form via deserialization. This section takes a closer look at data streams and object streams, both part of the **`java.io`** package, with implementation examples.

# [Data Streams](#toc.xhtml_s245a)

Java’s **`java.io`** package includes the **`DataInputStream`** and **`DataOutputStream`** classes. We can use methods in those classes to read and write primitive data types and Strings in a manner that is platform-agnostic. This helps ensure our code is portable. Common use cases for data streams are with networking applications and custom file types. The three primary features of data streams include platform independent, support primitive data types, and can support custom binary file formats.

*[Table 6.1](#c06.xhtml_tab6_1)* identifies the most commonly used methods from the **`DataInputStream`** and **`DataOutputStream`** classes.

| **Data Type** | **Input Method** | **Output Method** |
| Integer | **`readInt()`** | **`writeInt(int v)`** |
| Float | **`readFloat()`** | **`writeFloat(float v)`** |
| Long | **`readLong()`** | **`writeLong(long v)`** |
| String | **`readUTF()`** | **`writeUTF(String s)`** |
| Boolean | **`readBoolean()`** | **`writeBoolean(boolean v)`** |

**Table 6.1:** Common Data Stream Methods

Let’s look at an example application that writes and reads binary data using the **`DataInputStream`** and **`DataOutputStream`** classes.

`import java.io.DataInputStream;`

`import java.io.DataOutputStream;`

`import java.io.FileInputStream;`

`import java.io.FileOutputStream;`

`import java.io.IOException;`

`public class DataStreamExample {`

`public static void main(String[] args) {`

`String fileName = "myDataStreamExample.dat";`

`// Writing data using DataOutputStream`

`try (DataOutputStream dataOut = new DataOutputStream(new FileOutputStream(fileName))) {`

`dataOut.writeInt(319);`

`dataOut.writeFloat(3.19f);`

`dataOut.writeUTF("Data stream test.");`

`} catch (IOException e) {`

`System.out.println("Error writing data stream: " + e.getMessage());`

`}`

`// Reading data using DataInputStream`

`try (DataInputStream dataIn = new DataInputStream(new FileInputStream(fileName))) {`

`int number = dataIn.readInt();`

`float pi = dataIn.readFloat();`

`String message = dataIn.readUTF();`

`System.out.println("Values read: " + number + ", " + pi + ", " + message);`

`} catch (IOException e) {`

`System.out.println("Error reading data: " + e.getMessage());`

`}`

`}`

`}`

Our example starts by writing an integer, a float, and a string using methods from the **`DataOutputStream`** class to a binary file. The second part of the application uses methods from the **`DataInputStream`** class to read the stream in the same order it was written. This sequencing is important as it can help ensure we do not misinterpret the data. The output of the application is provided here:

`Values read: 319, 3.19, Data stream test.`

Next, let us take a look at object streams.

# [Object Streams](#toc.xhtml_s246a)

Java’s **`java.io`** package includes the **`ObjectInputStream`** an **`ObjectOutputStream`** classes that we can use to **serialize** and **deserialize** objects. **Serialization** is the process of converting an object to a byte stream and **deserialization** reverses the process. Common use cases for object streams are:

*   Transferring objects over a network
*   Saving object states
*   When working with complex data structures

These use cases also represent the key features of object streams:

*   We are able to share object streams over a network (that is, distributed systems).
*   We can safely save and object states between application sessions, resulting in object persistence.
*   We can store and transfer complex data.

*[Table 6.2](#c06.xhtml_tab6_2)* identifies the most commonly used methods from the **`ObjectInputStream`** and **`ObjectOutputStream`** classes.

| **Method** | **Purpose** |
| **`readObject(Object obj)`** | Reads and deserializes an object from an object stream. |
| **`writeObject(Object obj)`** | Serializes and writes an object to an object stream. |

**Table 6.2:** Common Object Stream Methods

Let’s look at an example application that serializes and deserializes an object. This example requires two classes. First, we will write a **`Cyborg`** class to define our object.

`import java.io.*;`

`class Cyborg implements Serializable {`

`private static final long serialVersionUID = 1L;`

`private String name;`

`private int assimilationAge;`

`public Cyborg(String name, int assimilationAge) {`

`this.name = name;`

`this.assimilationAge = assimilationAge;`

`}`

`@Override`

`public String toString() {`

`return "Cyborg{name='" + name + "', assimilationAge=" + assimilationAge + '}';`

`}`

`}`

Next, we will write an **`ObjectStreamExample`** class to serialize and deserialize a **`Cyborg`** object.

`import java.io.*;`

`public class ObjectStreamExample {`

`public static void main(String[] args) {`

`String fileName = "objectStreamExample.ser";`

`// Serializing the object`

`try (ObjectOutputStream objOut = new ObjectOutputStream(new FileOutputStream(fileName))) {`

`Cyborg cyborg = new Cyborg("Seven of Nine", 6);`

`objOut.writeObject(cyborg);`

`System.out.println("Object serialized: " + cyborg);`

`} catch (IOException e) {`

`System.out.println("Error serializing object: " + e.getMessage());`

`}`

`// Deserializing the object`

`try (ObjectInputStream objIn = new ObjectInputStream(new FileInputStream(fileName))) {`

`Cyborg cyborg = (Cyborg) objIn.readObject();`

`System.out.println("Object deserialized: " + cyborg);`

`} catch (IOException | ClassNotFoundException e) {`

`System.out.println("Error deserializing object: " + e.getMessage());`

`}`

`}`

`}`

As you can see in the example, our **`Cyborg`** class implemented the **`Serializable`** interface. That interface must be used for an object to be serialized. It is known as a marker interface because it does not contain any attributes or methods; instead, it simply marks a class with a specific property or behavior. In our example, the **`Serializable`** interface marks the **`Cyborg`** class, indicating Cyborg objects can be serialized.

The output of the application is provided here:

`Object serialized: Cyborg{name='Seven of Nine', assimilationAge=6}`

`Object deserialized: Cyborg{name='Seven of Nine', assimilationAge=6}`

# [Managing I/O Resources](#toc.xhtml_s247a)

Working with input and output streams requires specific attention to operational efficiency. Failing to properly handle resources, such as not closing files or streams, can result in the following outcomes:

*   System crash
*   Resource leaks
*   Performance degradation
*   User loss of confidence

Fortunately, Java makes the management of input/output (I/O) resources easy for us. We can use the **try-with-resources** statement to automatically close resources when they are no longer needed.

The **try-with-resources** statement is part of the **`java.lang.AutoCloseable`** interface. Using this interface ensures that any resource implementing **`AutoCloseable`** will be automatically closed at the end of the **`try`** block. This eliminates the need for manual resource cleanup in a **`finally`** block. Let us look at the syntax:

`try (ResourceType resource = new ResourceType()) {`

`// Resource usage goes here`

`} catch (ExceptionType e) {`

`// Exception handling goes here`

`}`

The **try-with-resources** statement is a variation of the **`try`** block that was introduced in *[Chapter 5, File and Exception Handling](#c05.xhtml)*. To use this statement, we declare one or more resources within the **`try`** statement’s parentheses. These resources will automatically be closed when the block is exited, even if an exception is the reason for exiting the block. In our context, a resource is any object that implements the **`AutoCloseable`** interface or the **`Closeable`** subclass.

The **try-with-resources** statement is typically used when handling file streams, network connections, database connections, and custom resources. Advantages of this technique include automatic resource management, simplified code, and the safe handling of exceptions.

# [File Streams](#toc.xhtml_s248a)

This section demonstrates how to use the try-with-resources statement with file I/O operations. Let us start with an example with reading a file.

`import java.io.BufferedReader;`

`import java.io.FileReader;`

`import java.io.IOException;`

`public class TryWithResourcesExample1 {`

`public static void main(String[] args) {`

`try (BufferedReader reader = new BufferedReader(new FileReader("myExample.txt"))) {`

`String line;`

`while ((line = reader.readLine()) != null) {`

`System.out.println(line);`

`}`

`} catch (IOException e) {`

`System.out.println("Error reading the file: " + e.getMessage());`

`}`

`}`

`}`

In this example, we declared a **`BufferedReader`** within the try-with-resources statement. While we do not see it, the **`BufferedReader`**'s **`close()`** method is automatically called when the block is exited. This ensures proper resource cleanup.Next, let us look at an example where we are writing to a file.

`import java.io.BufferedWriter;`

`import java.io.FileWriter;`

`import java.io.IOException;`

`public class TryWithResourcesExample2 {`

`public static void main(String[] args) {`

`try (BufferedWriter writer = new BufferedWriter(new FileWriter("myOutput2.txt"))) {`

`writer.write("Using try-with-resources to write to a file.");`

`} catch (IOException e) {`

`System.out.println("Error writing to the file: " + e.getMessage());`

`}`

`}`

`}`

In this example, we manage the **`BufferedWriter`** within the try-with-resources statement. This automatically closes the stream after the write operation is completed.

# [Multiple Resources](#toc.xhtml_s249a)

Java gives us flexibility in the management of I/O resources. Specifically, we can use the try-with resources statement with multiple resources in a single block. We simply separate each resource with a semicolon (**`;`**) inside the parentheses. This results in the closure of all resources in reverse order of how they were declared.

Let us look at an implementation with an application that copies a file.

`import java.io.BufferedInputStream;`

`import java.io.BufferedOutputStream;`

`import java.io.FileInputStream;`

`import java.io.FileOutputStream;`

`import java.io.IOException;`

`public class TryWithResourcesExampmle3 {`

`public static void main(String[] args) {`

`try (BufferedInputStream input = new BufferedInputStream(new FileInputStream("mySource3.txt"));`

`BufferedOutputStream output = new BufferedOutputStream(new FileOutputStream("myDestination3.txt"))) {`

`byte[] buffer = new byte[1024];`

`int bytesRead;`

`while ((bytesRead = input.read(buffer)) != -1) {`

`output.write(buffer, 0, bytesRead);`

`}`

`} catch (IOException e) {`

`System.out.println("Error during file copy: " + e.getMessage());`

`}`

`}`

`}`

In this example, we declared two resources (**`BufferedInputStream`** and **`BufferedOutputStream`**) within the same try-with-resources statement. Both streams are automatically closed when the block is exited.

# [Custom Resources](#toc.xhtml_s250a)

Java allows us to write custom resources that implement the **`AutoCloseable`** interface for use with the try-with-resources statement. We simply need to include a **`close()`** method in the custom resource class. Let us look at an example:

`class CustomResource implements AutoCloseable {`

`@Override`

`public void close() {`

`System.out.println("CustomResource is now closed.");`

`}`

`public void use() {`

`System.out.println("Using CustomResource .` `.` `.");`

`}`

`}`

Our custom class, **`CustomResource`**, implements **`AutoCloseable`**. Now, let us write a program to use our **`CustomResource`** in a try-with-resources statement.

`public class TryWithResourcesExample4 {`

`public static void main(String[] args) {`

`try (CustomResource resource = new CustomResource()) {`

`resource.use();`

`} catch (Exception e) {`

`System.out.println("Error: " + e.getMessage());`

`}`

`}`

`}`

In this example, the custom class **`close()`** method is automatically invoked at the end of the **`try`** block.

# Exception Handling

It is important to note that when exceptions occur within a try-with-resources block, they are passed along the method chain normally. If an exception occurs during the resource closing operation, it is suppressed. These suppressed exceptions can be retrieved by using the **`Throwable.getSuppressed()`** method. Let us look at an example:

`import java.io.*;`

`public class TryWithResourcesExample5 {`

`public static void main(String[] args) {`

`try (BufferedReader reader = new BufferedReader(new FileReader("thisFileDoesNotExist.txt"))) {`

`System.out.println(reader.readLine());`

`} catch (IOException e) {`

`System.out.println("Primary exception: " + e.getMessage());`

`for (Throwable suppressed : e.getSuppressed()) {`

`System.out.println("Suppressed exception: " + suppressed.getMessage());`

`}`

`}`

`}`

`}`

In this example, we demonstrated that if an exception occurs during the resource closing operation, it is suppressed. That suppressed error is obtainable via the **`e.getSuppressed()`** method. Here is the output of that application:

`Primary exception: thisFileDoesNotExist.txt (No such file or directory)`

# [Book Long Project](#toc.xhtml_s251a)

It is time to expand the SLAP LMS application you have worked on at the end of each of the previous chapters. In this section, we will explore how to improve the application’s data handling capabilities using Java’s input/output streams. You will be asked to implement byte streams for binary data, character streams for text-based data, and buffered streams to enhance performance. The goal is to help you enable efficient reading and writing of LMS data, making your application scalable and reliable.

# [Using Byte Streams for Binary Data](#toc.xhtml_s252a)

You should implement byte streams to handle raw, unprocessed binary data. For the SLAP LMS, this might be used to load and save images or multimedia content for courses.

Here is an example code:

`import java.io.FileInputStream;`

`import java.io.FileOutputStream;`

`import java.io.IOException;`

`public class ByteStreamExample {`

`public static void saveCourseBanner(String sourceFile, String destinationFile) {`

`try (FileInputStream input = new FileInputStream(sourceFile);`

`FileOutputStream output = new FileOutputStream(destinationFile)) {`

`byte[] buffer = new byte[1024];`

`int bytesRead;`

`while ((bytesRead = input.read(buffer)) != -1) {`

`output.write(buffer, 0, bytesRead);`

`}`

`} catch (IOException e) {`

`System.out.println("Error handling binary file: " + e.getMessage());`

`}`

`}`

`}`

# [Using Character Streams for Text Data](#toc.xhtml_s253a)

You can use character streams to handle text-based data, such as course descriptions or student names. This ensures proper encoding and decoding of text. You should update the **`Course`** class to save and retrieve course details using **`FileReader`** and **`FileWriter`**.

Here are example code snippets:

`writer.write(courseDetails);`

`} catch (IOException e) {`

`}`

`}`

`public static void loadCourseDetails(String fileName) {`

`int character;`

`while ((character = reader.read()) != -1) {`

`}`

`}`

`}`

# [Enhancing Performance with Buffered Streams](#toc.xhtml_s254a)

Buffered streams can be used to improve the performance of reading and writing operations, especially for large files. You should apply **`BufferedReader`** and **`BufferedWriter`** to manage student feedback or large course rosters.

Here are example code snippets:

`public static void saveFeedback(String feedback, String fileName) {`

# [Using Data Streams for Structured Data](#toc.xhtml_s255a)

Next, implement **`DataInputStream`** and **`DataOutputStream`** to save structured binary data, such as student scores or course statistics.

Here are example code snippets:

`public static void saveStudentScores(String fileName, int[] scores) {`

`try (DataOutputStream output = new DataOutputStream(new FileOutputStream(fileName))) {`

`for (int score : scores) {`

`output.writeInt(score);`

`}`

`} catch (IOException e) {`

`}`

`}`

`public static void loadStudentScores(String fileName) {`

`while (true) {`

`}`

`} catch (IOException e) {`

`}`

`}`

# [Serialization for Complex Objects](#toc.xhtml_s256a)

Next, use **`ObjectOutputStream`** and **`ObjectInputStream`** to serialize and deserialize **`Course`** objects, enabling efficient saving and loading of complex data structures.

Here are example code snippets:

`public static void saveCourseObject(Course course, String fileName) {`

`try (ObjectOutputStream output = new ObjectOutputStream(new FileOutputStream(fileName))) {`

`output.writeObject(course);`

`} catch (IOException e) {`

`System.out.println("Error serializing course: " + e.getMessage());`

`}`

`}`

`public static Course loadCourseObject(String fileName) {`

`try (ObjectInputStream input = new ObjectInputStream(new FileInputStream(fileName))) {`

`return (Course) input.readObject();`

`} catch (IOException | ClassNotFoundException e) {`

`System.out.println("Error deserializing course: " + e.getMessage());`

`return null;`

`}`

`}`

# [Managing Resources with `Try-With-Resources`](#toc.xhtml_s257a)

Lastly, take the necessary steps to implement efficient resource management. You can accomplish this by refactoring all I/O operations to use Java’s try-with-resources statement. This eliminates the need for manual resource closure and avoids potential resource leaks.

# [Conclusion](#toc.xhtml_s258a)

This chapter explored the fundamental concepts of Java’s input/output streams and demonstrated how to use them for handling data of various types. The distinctions between byte and character streams were covered to help you effectively manage raw binary data and text data, respectively. Examples of buffered streams were used to demonstrate how performance optimization can be achieved by reducing the frequency of I/O operations.

The chapter also explored data streams and object streams, which enable structured data handling and object serialization. These streams allow us to write robust code that stores and transmits data efficiently, and even maintain data precision and compatibility across platforms. Practical examples were provided, such as working with binary files and serializing objects, showcasing real-world use cases of these streams.

Finally, the chapter addressed resource management with Java’s try-with-resources statement, demonstrating the simplicity of implementing automatic I/O resource cleanup, even when exceptions occur. This feature reduces code complexity and also enhances application reliability by preventing resource leaks.

In the next chapter, we will look at how to create Graphical User Interfaces (GUIs) using JavaFX, a powerful framework for building modern, visually appealing applications. This coverage will include the basics of JavaFX, including layout management, event handling, and incorporating various UI components such as buttons, text fields, and menus. This chapter will also explore alternative GUI frameworks available in the Java ecosystem. You can learn the strengths and weaknesses of each framework and how to choose the right one for your project’s needs. Practical examples will demonstrate how to implement basic interfaces using these alternative tools. By the end of this chapter, you should be able to design and implement functional GUI applications.

# [Points to Remember](#toc.xhtml_s259a)

*   Abstract classes can have both abstract and concrete methods, instance variables, and constructors.
*   A byte stream processes raw binary data, handling it one byte at a time without character encoding or interpretation.
*   **`BufferedInputStream`** and **`BufferedOutputStream`** enhance the performance of byte streams by reading and writing data in larger chunks.
*   **`BufferedReader`** and **`BufferedWriter`** enhance character stream performance and include methods such as **`readLine()`** and **`newLine().`**
*   Buffered streams improve I/O performance by reducing the number of read and write operations through temporary storage in memory.
*   Closing resources such as streams is critical to preventing memory leaks, resource exhaustion, and degraded application performance.
*   **`DataInputStream`** and **`DataOutputStream`** classes provide platform-independent methods to read and write primitive types and Strings in binary format.
*   **`FileReader`** and **`FileWriter`** handle character data, making them suitable for working with text files and managing character encoding automatically.
*   Flushing a buffered output stream ensures all data in the buffer is written immediately to the destination, which is essential in real-time and network applications.
*   **`InputStream`** and **`OutputStream`** are abstract classes forming the foundation for all byte-based data processing in Java.
*   Java organizes its I/O classes hierarchically, with abstract classes such as **`Reader`**, **`Writer`**, **`InputStream`**, and **`OutputStream`** serving as foundational classes.
*   **`ObjectInputStream`** and **`ObjectOutputStream`** enable serialization and deserialization of objects, converting them to and from a byte stream.
*   **`Reader`** and **`Writer`** classes are abstract classes designed to handle character-based data, supporting text file operations and Unicode encoding.
*   Resources declared in a try-with-resources block are automatically closed when the block exits, even if an exception occurs.
*   Serialization is the process of converting an object into a byte stream for storage or transmission, while deserialization reconstructs the object from the byte stream.
*   Streams in Java are unidirectional, meaning a single stream handles either input or output, but not both.
*   The **`AutoCloseable`** interface is implemented by resources that can be automatically closed using try-with-resources.
*   The default buffer size in Java streams is 8 KB, but it can be adjusted based on application requirements for improved performance.
*   The **`flush()`** method ensures that buffered data is sent immediately to its destination, preventing delays in output.
*   The **`Serializable`** interface is a marker interface required for a class to support serialization.
*   `try-with-resources` is an efficient way to manage resources such as streams, sockets, and database connections, reducing boilerplate code.
*   Writing data with **`ObjectOutputStream`** requires that the class of the object being serialized implements the **`Serializable`** interface.

# [Multiple-Choice Questions](#toc.xhtml_s260a)

1.  What is the primary purpose of buffering in Java I/O streams?
    1.  To simplify stream implementation
    2.  To reduce the number of read and write operations
    3.  To enhance character encoding
    4.  To increase the size of the data source
2.  Which Java classes are used to serialize and deserialize objects?
    1.  `DataInputStream` and `DataOutputStream`
    2.  `FileReader` and `FileWriter`
    3.  `ObjectInputStream` and `ObjectOutputStream`
    4.  `BufferedReader` and `BufferedWriter`
3.  Which of the following is a key feature of try-with-resources?
    1.  Allows for managing multiple resources in a single block
    2.  Requires manual resource closing
    3.  Works only with file streams
    4.  Automatically suppresses exceptions thrown with the block
4.  What is the purpose of Java’s `Serializable` interface?
    1.  To mark a class as suitable for serialization
    2.  To handle platform-independent character encoding
    3.  To facilitate resource management with I/O operations
    4.  To enable primitive data type handing in streams
5.  What happens when the `flush()` method is called on a buffered output stream?
    1.  It resets the buffer to its initial size
    2.  It immediately writes all buffered data to the destination
    3.  It closes the stream and releases all associated resources
    4.  It reads data from the input source and fills the buffer

# [Answers](#toc.xhtml_s261a)

1.  b
2.  c
3.  a
4.  a
5.  b

# [Key Terms](#toc.xhtml_s263a)

*   **`AutoCloseable`**: An interface that allows resources to be automatically closed when used with try-with-resources.
*   **`BufferedInputStream`**: A class that enhances the performance of **`InputStream`** by reading data in larger chunks into a memory buffer.
*   **`BufferedOutputStream`**: A class that enhances the performance of **`OutputStream`** by writing data in larger chunks from a memory buffer.
*   **`BufferedReader`**: A class that enhances the performance of **`Reader`** by reading text data in larger chunks and providing convenient methods such as **`readLine()`**.
*   **`BufferedWriter`**: A class that enhances the performance of **`Writer`** by writing text data in larger chunks and providing methods such as **`newLine()`**.
*   **DataInputStream**: A class used to read primitive data types and Strings in a binary format from an input stream.
*   **`DataOutputStream`**: A class used to write primitive data types and Strings in a binary format to an output stream.
*   **Deserialization**: The process of reconstructing an object from a serialized byte stream.
*   **`FileReader`**: A class used to read character data from text files.
*   **`FileWriter`**: A class used to write character data to text files.
*   **Flush**: A method that forces all buffered data in an output stream to be written immediately to its destination.
*   **`InputStream`**: An abstract class that provides a foundation for reading raw binary data as bytes.
*   **`ObjectInputStream`**: A class used to deserialize objects by reading them from a byte stream.
*   **`ObjectOutputStream`**: A class used to serialize objects by converting them into a byte stream.
*   **`OutputStream`**: An abstract class that provides a foundation for writing raw binary data as bytes.
*   **Reader**: An abstract class that provides a foundation for reading character data.
*   **Serializable**: A marker interface used to indicate that a class can be serialized.
*   **Serialization**: The process of converting an object into a byte stream for storage or transmission.
*   **try-with-resources**: A Java construct that simplifies resource management by automatically closing resources declared in the try block.
*   **Writer**: An abstract class that provides a foundation for writing character data.

# [Exercises](#toc.xhtml_s264a)

**Exercise 1: Reading and Writing Text Files**

**Objective**: Practice using character streams to handle text data in Java.

**Activity**: Write a Java program that reads the contents of a text file named **`input.txt`** using **`FileReader`** and writes its contents to another file named **`output.txt`** using **`FileWriter`**. Include error handling to manage missing files or I/O errors.

**Exercise 2: Using Buffered Streams for Efficiency**

**Objective**: Understand how buffered streams improve I/O performance.

**Activity**: Create a Java program that reads data from a large text file using both **`BufferedReader`** and **`FileReader`**. Measure the time taken for each approach and compare their performance. Write a brief reflection on the results.

**Exercise 3: Implementing Object Serialization**

**Objective**: Learn how to serialize and deserialize Java objects.

**Activity**: Define a class **`Student`** with fields for **`name`**, **`age`**, and **`GPA`**. Write a Java program that serializes an object of this class to a file named **`student.ser`** using **`ObjectOutputStream`** and then deserializes it using **`ObjectInputStream`**. Display the object’s data before and after serialization to verify correctness.

**Exercise 4: Custom Resources**

**Objective**: Implement a custom resource class that integrates with try-with-resources.

**Activity**: Create a class **`CustomLogger`** that implements **`AutoCloseable`** and simulates writing log messages to a file. Ensure the **`close()`** method writes a final message like "**`Logger closed`**." Demonstrate the use of this class in a program where the resource is managed automatically.

**Exercise 5: Handling Binary Data with Data Streams**

**Objective**: Practice working with binary data using data streams.

**Activity**: Write a program that uses **`DataOutputStream`** to write an integer, a floating-point number, and a UTF-8 string to a file named **`data.bin`**. Then, use **`DataInputStream`** to read the data back and display it on the console. Ensure proper sequencing of read and write operations.

# [CHAPTER 7](#toc.xhtml_c07)

# [GUI Programming](#toc.xhtml_c07)

# [Introduction](#toc.xhtml_s265a)

Ensuring that our applications work the way they are supposed to is a baseline expectation. Users expect software to work, but that is not enough. We also need to design and develop our applications so they are user-friendly and visually appealing. Those characteristics are key to the success of modern software. This chapter introduces Graphical User Interfaces (GUIs) in Java. We will focus on JavaFX, which is a powerful tool for building interactive Java applications.

We begin with the exploration of JavaFX fundamentals, including its architecture, components, and layout management tools such as VBox, HBox, and GridPane. Practical examples will be used to help guide you in creating responsive and interactive user interfaces. Beyond the visual component, we will also demonstrate event handling concepts to help make our applications interactive.

Building on these foundations, we will look at advanced JavaFX features such as multimedia and animation. Additionally, we will explore GUI frameworks as alternatives to JavaFX, including Abstract Window Toolkit (AWT), Standard Widget Toolkit (SWT), and web-based frameworks including JavaServer Faces (JSF) and Vaadin. We will compare these frameworks so we have a clear understanding of their strengths, weaknesses, and ideal use cases.

The practical examples and comparative insights provided in this chapter are intended to equip you with the knowledge and skills to design and implement functional GUIs using the right tools for your project. These are applicable to desktop and web-based interfaces.

By the end of this chapter, you should be able to understand the role and significance of GUI programming in modern applications, and explain the architecture and key features of JavaFX. You will learn to set up a JavaFX development environment in your IDE, design user interfaces using JavaFX components and layout managers such as VBox, HBox, and GridPane, and implement event handling to create interactive JavaFX applications. Furthermore, you will understand how to incorporate multimedia and animations into JavaFX projects. The chapter will also enable you to identify the key features of AWT, SWT, and web-based frameworks such as JSF and Vaadin, and build simple GUIs using AWT and SWT frameworks. You will also design and implement web-based user interfaces using JSF and Vaadin, compare the strengths, weaknesses, and use cases of JavaFX, AWT, SWT, and Java web frameworks, and select the appropriate GUI framework for a given project based on its requirements.

# [Structure](#toc.xhtml_s266a)

In this chapter, the following topics will be covered:

*   Introduction to GUI Programming
*   JavaFX Fundamentals
*   Advanced JavaFX Features
*   Alternative GUI Frameworks
*   GUI Framework Comparison

# [Introduction to GUI Programming](#toc.xhtml_s267a)

**Graphical User Interfaces (GUIs)** are an integral part of modern software. We want our users to interact with our software in a manner that is intuitive, appealing, and easy. The graphic component of these interfaces moves from text-based interactions to a more visually appealing system that allows users to interact with our software. We accomplish this by leveraging visual elements such as buttons, menus, and sliders to perform actions seamlessly.

This section explores the concept of GUI programming, the frameworks available in Java for creating GUIs, and why mastering GUI development is critical for modern Java developers.

# [Overview of GUI Frameworks](#toc.xhtml_s268a)

There are several frameworks available to us for creating GUIs, each with a unique set of features and capabilities. There is no single framework that is applicable for every use case, necessitating the need to understand at least the most prevalent frameworks. Once we have a firm understanding of these frameworks, we can select the one most appropriate for our project.

Here is a brief overview of the most popular GUI frameworks available to us for our Java applications. Each will be explored thoroughly later in the chapter.

# [JavaFX](#toc.xhtml_s269a)

**JavaFX** is the de facto standard for Java GUI development. It provides advanced components, layouts, and support for multimedia and animations, making it ideal for visually rich applications. JavaFX also supports web rendering and 3D graphics, broadening the scope of what we can achieve. JavaFX is the preferred modern GUI toolkit for new desktop applications, offering a more contemporary look and feel compared to its predecessors.

# [Abstract Window Toolkit (AWT)](#toc.xhtml_s270a)

**The Abstract Window Toolkit (AWT)** is one of the original GUI frameworks available for Java applications. AWT is a simple framework and limited in functionality and flexibility. It has a heavy reliance on the underlying operating system, which can lead to inconsistencies across different platforms. Despite its limitations, AWT laid the groundwork for more advanced frameworks and is still used for basic applications due to its straightforward nature.

# [Standard Widget Toolkit (SWT)](#toc.xhtml_s271a)

**The Standard Widget Toolkit (SWT)** framework was designed as an alternative to AWT. SWT is highly customizable and integrates more closely with native OS components. This framework is commonly used in enterprise applications. SWT’s approach of leveraging native widgets provides better performance and a more native user experience. It is a core part of the **Eclipse IDE**, demonstrating its robustness and capability in handling complex GUI requirements.

# [Web-Based Frameworks](#toc.xhtml_s272a)

**Web-based frameworks** such as **JavaServer Faces (JSF)** and **Vaadin**, extend GUI programming to web applications. JSF enables server-side rendering of web pages, and Vaadin allows us to build interactive web applications with Java code. These frameworks facilitate the creation of dynamic and responsive web interfaces, bridging the gap between traditional desktop GUI frameworks and modern web development. They provide extensive libraries and tools to streamline the development process, making them popular choices for enterprise-level web applications.

Each framework has its strengths, weaknesses, and specific use cases, which we will explore later in this chapter. Understanding the features of these frameworks can help you select the right one for your project’s needs.

# [Benefits of GUI Programming](#toc.xhtml_s273a)

GUIs connect our users to our application’s functionality. It should not be considered a mere enhancement; rather, GUIs are an essential part of most modern Java applications. Here are the primary benefits and reasons why GUI programming remains relevant today:

*   **Accessibility:** GUIs provide visual and interactive elements that should help users navigate software without relying on text-based commands.
*   **Enhanced User Experience:** GUIs make applications easier and more enjoyable to use. They should accommodate users who may not have technical expertise.
*   **Market Demand:** As the software market grows, so does the need for developers skilled in creating robust and appealing GUIs. Proficiency in GUI development is an important skillset which can set you apart as a versatile developer capable of handling both back-end and front-end needs.
*   **Productivity:** GUIs are essential in industries such as healthcare, education, and retail, where user-friendly interfaces are crucial for productivity and engagement.
*   **Versatility:** GUIs play a critical role in ensuring broad user adoption and satisfaction. This is true for web, mobile, and desktop applications.

There is an adage that states if your software requires a user manual, then your GUI was not designed intuitively enough. As you progress through this chapter, you should gain a solid foundation in Java GUI programming, equipping you to create intuitive and professional-looking applications for a wide range of use cases.

# [JavaFX Fundamentals](#toc.xhtml_s274a)

**JavaFX** is a robust framework that facilitates building visually rich and interactive GUIs in Java. It provides us with tools and capabilities to design professional interfaces for our desktop applications. This section explains the foundational aspects of JavaFX, guides you through setting it up in your development environment, and provides examples of layout management and event handling.

# [Introduction to JavaFX and its Architecture](#toc.xhtml_s275a)

Developing GUIs for our Java applications is facilitated by JavaFX’s powerful toolkit. JavaFX’s architecture is designed to help us rapidly build GUIs for our applications. Key components of the JavaFX architecture include:

*   **CSS Styling:** JavaFX supports **Cascading Style Sheets** (**CSS**) for customizing the appearance of UI components. This empowers us to build rich and consistent visual designs.
*   **Event-Driven Programming:** JavaFX handles user interactions through event-driven programming, such as when a button is clicked. This enables seamless and intuitive functionality.
*   **FXML:** FXML is a declarative **eXtensible Markup Language** (**XML**)-based markup language for designing GUIs. It separates design from logic, which promotes more readable code, improving developer-designer collaboration.
*   **Nodes:** Every visual element in JavaFX is a **node**. These UI elements include buttons, labels, text fields, images, and more.
*   **Stage and Scene:** These are the GUI canvas. The stage represents the primary window, and the scene holds all the visual components.

Each of these JavaFX architectural components will be explored further later in this chapter.

    `package application;`
