# [Key Terms](#toc.xhtml_s675a)

*   **Activity Lifecycle:** The sequence of states an Android application goes through, including creation, start, resume, pause, stop, and destruction.
*   **Android Emulator:** A tool in Android Studio that simulates an Android device for testing applications without requiring physical hardware.
*   **AndroidManifest.xml:** An Android project configuration file that defines app properties such as activities, permissions, and configurations.
*   **Build.gradle:** A configuration file in Android projects that manages dependencies, build settings, and application modules.
*   **Cross-Platform Development:** The practice of writing a single codebase that can be deployed on multiple platforms, such as Android and iOS.
*   **Data Persistence:** The ability of an application to store and retrieve data across multiple sessions, ensuring user data is not lost when the app is closed.
*   **Event Handling:** The process of managing user interactions, such as button clicks and gestures, within an application.
*   **Gradle:** A build automation tool used in Android Studio to compile source code, manage dependencies, and generate APK files.
*   **Java Virtual Machine (JVM):** The runtime environment that executes Java bytecode, though Android applications typically run on ART instead of the JVM.
*   **MainActivity:** The entry point of an Android application.
*   **Model-View-ViewModel (MVVM):** A software design pattern that separates UI logic from business logic to create more maintainable applications.
*   **Native Development:** The process of developing applications using platform-specific languages and tools, such as Java and Android Studio for Android apps.
*   **React Native:** A cross-platform framework that allows developers to build mobile applications using JavaScript or TypeScript.
*   **SharedPreferences:** A lightweight data storage mechanism in Android that allows key-value pairs to be saved and retrieved across app sessions.
*   **TextView:** A UI component in Android used to display text within an application layout.
*   **User Interaction:** The ways in which a user engages with an application, including taps, swipes, and text input.
*   **ViewModel:** An Android architecture component that stores UI-related data and survives configuration changes such as screen rotations.
*   **XML Layouts:** Files in Android development used to define the structure and appearance of user interfaces separately from Java logic.

# [CHAPTER 18](#toc.xhtml_c18)

# [Design Patterns in Java](#toc.xhtml_c18)

# [Introduction](#toc.xhtml_s677a)

Design patterns are proven and reusable solutions to common problems specific to software design. While design patterns are not specific to Java, we will cover them in the context of Java. These proven solutions provide us with patterns, or blueprints to guide our own software design decisions. Using design patterns saves us considerable development time and makes our code more readable and maintainable.

This chapter explores several foundational design patterns based on the Gang of Four (GoF) classifications of creational, structural, and behavioral. We will cover several design patterns in each of the GoF classifications and demonstrate key patterns with Java-based implementations.

By the end of this chapter, you should be able to explain the role of design patterns in Java software development, explain the three main categories of design patterns, implement common creational patterns in Java, and apply structural patterns. Furthermore, you will learn to use behavioral patterns in Java, evaluate when to use specific design patterns in Java projects, and recognize trade-offs involved in using design patterns.

# [Structure](#toc.xhtml_s678a)

In this chapter, the following topics will be covered:

*   Introduction to Design Patterns
*   Creational Patterns
*   Structural Patterns
*   Behavioral Patterns
*   Apply Design Patterns in Java Projects

# [Introduction to Design Patterns](#toc.xhtml_s679a)

The use of **design patterns** helps make our systems robust, scalable, and easy to maintain. The appropriate implementation of design patterns can significantly improve the quality of our code and streamline the development process.

Think of software design patterns like sewing patterns. If you need to create a pair of bell-bottom pants for a male, you do not have to start from scratch, you can use a sewing pattern. Just as the sewing patterns are blueprints for the seamstress, saving them considerable time, a software design pattern will save software developers considerable time, as they use a blueprint instead of starting from scratch.

No discussion of software design patterns is complete without mention of the **Gang of Four** (**GoF**). Their 1994 book is referenced below:

Gamma, E., Helm, R., Johnson, R., & Vlissides, J. (1994). *Design patterns: Elements of reusable object-oriented software*. Addison-Wesley Professional.

It is important to note that software design patterns are programming language agnostic. They are most useful when implemented in object-oriented languages such as Java.

# [Benefits](#toc.xhtml_s680a)

We already established that using design patterns saves us a lot of development time. They also give us the confidence to know that our solution is already proven to work. Additional benefits include:

*   Code reusability
*   Increased maintainability
*   Consistency across projects
*   Increased team communication (based on knowledge of patterns)

The larger the system you are creating, the greater benefits you stand to reap using design patterns.

# [Categories](#toc.xhtml_s681a)

There are three primary design pattern categories, each addressing a different aspect of object-oriented software development. The categories of **creational**, **structural**, and **behavioral** are previewed in *[Table 18.1](#c18.xhtml_tab18_1)* and covered in this section.

| **Category** | **Focus** |
| Creational | Object creation |
| Structural | Relationships between classes and objects |
| Behavioral | Communication between objects |

**Table 18.1:** Overview of Major Design Pattern Categories

# [Creational Patterns](#toc.xhtml_s682a)

**Creational patterns** are focused on how we create objects. The main premise is to abstract the object instantiation process so our systems can be more flexible. Specifically, we want our systems to determine which objects to create as well as how to create them.

The following creational patterns will be covered later in this chapter with examples:

*   **Singleton:** A design pattern that ensures that only one instance of a class can exist.
*   **Factory:** This design pattern provides an interface for creating objects without having to specify the exact class.

These creational design patterns were selected from an extensive list as they are the most used.

# [Structural Patterns](#toc.xhtml_s683a)

**Structural patterns** help uncomplicate our code by providing simple ways to connect entities (for example, classes and objects). These design patterns focus on how classes and objects are grouped to form larger software structures.

The following structural patterns will be covered later in this chapter with examples:

*   **Adapter:** This design pattern enables incompatible interfaces to work together.
*   **Decorator:** This design pattern dynamically adds responsibilities to objects.

There are several more structural design patterns available to us. The ones listed below are among the most used.

# [Behavioral Patterns](#toc.xhtml_s684a)

**Behavioral patterns** define how objects communicate with each other. This includes delegating responsibilities among themselves.

The following behavioral patterns will be covered later in this chapter with examples:

*   **Observer:** This design pattern defines a one-to-many dependency between objects. This ensures that when one object changes state, all its dependents will be notified.
*   **Strategy:** This design pattern enables runtime selection of an algorithm’s behavior.

These behavioral design patterns were selected from an extensive list as they are the most used.

# [Creational Patterns](#toc.xhtml_s685a)

Creational patterns, as we previously indicated, abstract the object instantiation process. The goal is to make systems independent of how their objects are created. We will explore the two most common creational patterns, singleton and factory, in this section. For consistency, our examples will have the context of a fictional television network application.

# [Singleton Pattern](#toc.xhtml_s686a)

The **singleton pattern**, true to its name, ensures that there can only be one instance of a class. It also ensures that there is global access to the singleton class. We might implement this design pattern when we only need one object of a class to coordinate system actions.

In the context of a television network system, we will create **`BroadcastScheduler`** as a singleton class responsible for managing and scheduling programs across all channels. Given that use case, we would not want multiple instances of this scheduler running simultaneously. It would most assuredly result in conflicts.

Here is our **`BroadcastScheduler`** class:

`// Singleton class`

`public class BroadcastScheduler {`

`// Private static instance`

`private static BroadcastScheduler instance;`

`// Private constructor prevents external instantiation`

`private BroadcastScheduler() {`

`System.out.println("BroadcastScheduler initialized.");`

`}`

`// Public method to provide global access point`

`public static BroadcastScheduler getInstance() {`

`if (instance == null) {`

`instance = new BroadcastScheduler();`

`}`

`return instance;`

`}`

`// Example method to simulate scheduling`

`public void scheduleProgram(String channel, String program, String time) {`

`System.out.println("Scheduled '" + program + "' on " + channel + " at " + time);`

`}`

`}`

Next, we will write a **`TVNetworkApp`** class that contains a **`main()`** method.

`class TVNetworkApp {`

`public static void main(String[] args) {`

`// Get Singleton instance and schedule a program`

`BroadcastScheduler scheduler = BroadcastScheduler.getInstance();`

`scheduler.scheduleProgram("Channel 5", "Morning News", "7:00 AM");`

`// Get the Singleton instance again and schedule another program`

`BroadcastScheduler anotherScheduler = BroadcastScheduler.getInstance();`

`anotherScheduler.scheduleProgram("Channel 7", "Evening Show", "8:00 PM");`

`// Confirm both references are the same instance`

`System.out.println("Same instance?` `" + (scheduler == anotherScheduler)); // should print true`

`}`

`}`

Here is the output from this program:

`BroadcastScheduler initialized.`

`Scheduled 'Morning News' on Channel 5 at 7:00 AM`

`Scheduled 'Evening Show' on Channel 7 at 8:00 PM`

`Same instance?` `true`

# [Use Cases and Considerations](#toc.xhtml_s687a)

There are several instances when the use of this design pattern is appropriate, including the following:

*   Centralized configuration management
*   Logging mechanisms
*   Thread pools
*   Cache systems
*   Schedulers (as seen in our example)

The singleton design pattern can be extremely beneficial to us and our systems. When implementing this pattern, we should consider the following:

*   Singleton classes can behave like a global variable, making unit testing (see *[Chapter 13, Security, Testing, and Debugging](#c13.xhtml)* for information on unit testing) difficult.
*   Code maintainability could suffer because of hidden dependencies.
*   Our **`TVNetworkApp`** implementation is not thread-safe. If you are operating in a multi-threaded environment, you will want to use synchronization (see *[Chapter 8, Concurrency and Multi-Threading](#c08.xhtml)* for additional information).

# [Factory Pattern](#toc.xhtml_s688a)

Although it might seem impossible, we can create objects without having to specify the originating class. That is what the **factory pattern** gives us. It delegates the instantiation process to a class or method that is specifically designed for object creation.

There are two types of factory design pattern: **simple factory** and **factory method**. The simple factory makes a single class responsible for creating all the application’s objects, regardless of type. The factory method makes use of inheritance, allowing subclasses to decide which class to instantiate. This is done by overriding the factory method. We will demonstrate both types of this design pattern in this section.

Using our television network application as an example, consider a scenario where different types of TV programs need to be created (for example, news, sports, comedy, drama, and so on). Instead of using the **`new`** keyword to instantiate each one, a factory method can centralize our creation logic.

We will first demonstrate a simple factory. Let us start by creating a **`TVProgram`** interface:

`public interface TVProgram {`

`void play();`

`}`

Next, we will create four concrete classes, one for each type of television program:

`class NewsProgram implements TVProgram {`

`public void play() {`

`System.out.println("Now broadcasting: News Program");`

`}`

`}`

`class SportsProgram implements TVProgram {`

`public void play() {`

`System.out.println("Now broadcasting: Sports Program");`

`}`

`}`

`class ComedyProgram implements TVProgram {`

`public void play() {`

`System.out.println("Now broadcasting: Comedy Series");`

`}`

`}`

`class DramaProgram implements TVProgram {`

`public void play() {`

`System.out.println("Now broadcasting: Drama Series");`

`}`

`}`

Now we can write our simple factory class:

`public class ProgramFactory {`

`public static TVProgram createProgram(String type) {`

`switch (type.toLowerCase()) {`

`case "news": return new NewsProgram();`

`case "sports": return new SportsProgram();`

`case "drama": return new DramaProgram();`

`default: throw new IllegalArgumentException("Unknown program type: " + type);`

`}`

`}`

`}`

Lastly, we will create a program with a **`main()`** method so we can run and test our application.

`public class SimpleFactoryExample {`

`public static void main(String[] args) {`

`TVProgram news = ProgramFactory.createProgram("news");`

`TVProgram sports = ProgramFactory.createProgram("sports");`

`news.play();`

`sports.play();`

`}`

`}`

Here is the output from this program:

`Now broadcasting: News Program`

`Now broadcasting: Sports Program`

Now, let us demonstrate a factory method example. We will start with an abstract creator class:

`abstract class Channel {`

`public abstract TVProgram createProgram();`

`}`

Next, we will create two concrete creators, each for a different television channel.

`class NewsChannel extends Channel {`

`public TVProgram createProgram() {`

`return new NewsProgram();`

`}`

`}`

`class SportsChannel extends Channel {`

`public TVProgram createProgram() {`

`return new SportsProgram();`

`}`

`}`

Lastly, we need a program with a **`main()`** method so we can run and test our application.

`public class FactoryMethodExample {`

`public static void main(String[] args) {`

`Channel newsChannel = new NewsChannel();`

`TVProgram news = newsChannel.createProgram();`

`news.play();`

`Channel sportsChannel = new SportsChannel();`

`TVProgram sports = sportsChannel.createProgram();`

`sports.play();`

`}`

`}`

Here is the output from this program:

`Now broadcasting: News Program`

`Now broadcasting: Sports Program`

# [Use Cases and Considerations](#toc.xhtml_s689a)

There are several instances when the use of this design pattern is appropriate, including the following:

*   When object creation logic is complex
*   When object creation logic varies based on conditions
*   When your system should be open to new object types without modifying existing code
*   Logging frameworks
*   JDBC drivers

The factory design pattern can be extremely beneficial to us and our systems. When implementing this pattern, we can gain the following benefits:

*   Our application’s object creation will be simplified
*   Code readability will increase
*   Unit testing is possible because of the decoupling of client code and concrete implementations
*   Our application will be more extendable

# [Structural Patterns](#toc.xhtml_s690a)

**Structural patterns** are aptly named as they are focused on the architecture of our programs; specifically, how classes and objects are part of the overall system. These patterns help us design flexible and efficient systems by simplifying component relationships. This section demonstrates two core structural patterns: adapter and decorator. We will show how these patterns could be useful in a large system, such as our television network system’s backend.

# [Adapter Pattern](#toc.xhtml_s691a)

The **adapter pattern** connects to interfaces that otherwise would be incompatible. This pattern is like a bridge and a translator. We can use the adapter pattern to enable classes with mismatched interfaces to work together. This is often used when we need to integrate new systems with legacy code or external libraries.

Let us demonstrate this pattern using our TV network scenario. Imagine that our TV network wants to switch external weather forecast providers. The new provider has a different interface than our internal **`WeatherDisplay`** system expects. Instead of rewriting either system, we can create an adapter.

Our first class simulates a third-party weather service that is incompatible with our system.

`public class ExternalWeatherService {`

`public String getWeatherData() {`

`return "Sunny, 75°F";`

`}`

`}`

Next, here is our internal interface:

`public interface WeatherProvider {`

`String fetchForecast();`

`}`

Now we can write an adapter class that bridges and translates between our internal interface (**`WeatherProvider`**) and the third-party service (**`ExternalWeatherService`**).

`public class WeatherAdapter implements WeatherProvider {`

`private ExternalWeatherService externalService;`

`public WeatherAdapter(ExternalWeatherService service) {`

`this.externalService = service;`

`}`

`@Override`

`public String fetchForecast() {`

`// Adapting the external method to our internal method signature`

`return externalService.getWeatherData();`

`}`

`}`

Lastly, we need a program with a **`main()`** method so we can run and test our application.

`public class AdapterPatternExample {`

`public static void main(String[] args) {`

`ExternalWeatherService external = new ExternalWeatherService();`

`WeatherProvider adapter = new WeatherAdapter(external);`

`System.out.println("Today's Forecast: " + adapter.fetchForecast());`

`}`

`}`

Here is the output from this program:

`Today's Forecast: Sunny, 75°F`

# [Use Cases and Considerations](#toc.xhtml_s692a)

There are several instances when the use of this design pattern is appropriate, including the following:

*   You want to use an existing class whose interface does not match what you need.
*   You are integrating legacy code.
*   You are integrating a third-party system into your application.

The adapter design pattern can be extremely beneficial to us and our systems. When implementing this pattern, we should consider that int enables code reusability without altering existing classes.

# [Decorator Pattern](#toc.xhtml_s693a)

The **decorator pattern** allows us to dynamically add new functionality to objects at runtime. This is accomplished without altering the underlying class. In essence, we wrap the original object with a decorator class. This is a much cleaner solution than subclassing for behavior extension.

To demonstrate this design pattern, we will address the scenario that we want to broadcast TV programs with optional enhancements such as live captions or parental content warnings. Instead of subclassing every possible combination, we can use decorators.

We start with our **`TVProgram`** interface:

`public interface TVProgram {`

`void play();`

`}`

Next is a base class:

`public class BasicProgram implements TVProgram {`

`private String title;`

`public BasicProgram(String title) {`

`this.title = title;`

`}`

`@Override`

`public void play() {`

`System.out.println("Playing: " + title);`

`}`

`}`

Next, we need our abstract decorator:

`public abstract class ProgramDecorator implements TVProgram {`

`protected TVProgram program;`

`public ProgramDecorator(TVProgram program) {`

`this.program = program;`

`}`

`public void play() {`

`program.play();`

`}`

`}`

The code below includes two concrete decorators (one for each broadcast enhancement):

`public class CaptionDecorator extends ProgramDecorator {`

`public CaptionDecorator(TVProgram program) {`

`super(program);`

`}`

`@Override`

`public void play() {`

`super.play();`

`System.out.println("[Captions Enabled]");`

`}`

`}`

`public class WarningDecorator extends ProgramDecorator {`

`public WarningDecorator(TVProgram program) {`

`super(program);`

`}`

`@Override`

`public void play() {`

`System.out.println("[Parental Advisory: Some content may be inappropriate]");`

`super.play();`

`}`

`}`

Lastly, we need a program with a **`main()`** method so we can run and test our application.

`public class DecoratorPatternExample {`

`public static void main(String[] args) {`

`TVProgram program = new BasicProgram("Science Documentary");`

`// Add parental warning`

`program = new WarningDecorator(program);`

`// Add captions`

`program = new CaptionDecorator(program);`

`program.play();`

`}`

`}`

Here is the output from this program:

`[Parental Advisory: Some content may be inappropriate]`

`Playing: Science Documentary`

`[Captions Enabled]`

# [Use Cases and Considerations](#toc.xhtml_s694a)

There are several instances when the use of this design pattern is appropriate, including the following:

*   You want to add responsibilities to objects without modifying their class.
*   You want to avoid a large hierarchy of subclasses.

The decorator design pattern can be extremely beneficial to us and our systems. When implementing this pattern, we should consider that it promotes composition over inheritance and allows us to implement runtime behavior enhancement.

# [Behavioral Patterns](#toc.xhtml_s695a)

Our third design pattern category is **behavioral patterns**. They define how objects communicate and work with each other. These patterns focus on aspects such as:

*   Flow control
*   Responsibility delegation
*   Component runtime behavior

Our television network scenario is dynamic and could benefit greatly from implementing behavioral patterns. Our network’s content, user interactions, and schedules are constantly changing. Use of these patterns could enable flexibility and scalability.

This section introduces two essential behavioral patterns: observer and strategy.

# [Observer Pattern](#toc.xhtml_s696a)

The **observer pattern** creates a one-to-many dependency between objects. The purpose of this is to ensure that when one object’s state changes, all dependents are automatically notified. The primary object (the one) is referred to as the **subject** and the **dependents** (the many) are referred to as **observers**. This pattern is ideal for event-driven programming implementations and publish/subscribe schemas.

In our TV network scenario, we will implement a breaking news alert system. When breaking news is published, all registered subscribers (for example, the mobile app, website, social media bot, and so on) should automatically receive the alert.

We start with creating an interface for our subject:

`public interface NewsPublisher {`

`void subscribe(NewsObserver observer);`

`void unsubscribe(NewsObserver observer);`

`void notifySubscribers(String news);`

`}`

Next, we create a concrete subject:

`import java.util.*;`

`public class BreakingNewsAgency implements NewsPublisher {`

`private List<NewsObserver> subscribers = new ArrayList<>();`

`@Override`

`public void subscribe(NewsObserver observer) {`

`subscribers.add(observer);`

`}`

`@Override`

`public void unsubscribe(NewsObserver observer) {`

`subscribers.remove(observer);`

`}`

`@Override`

`public void notifySubscribers(String news) {`

`for (NewsObserver observer : subscribers) {`

`observer.update(news);`

`}`

`}`

`}`

We will also need an observer interface:

`public interface NewsObserver {`

`void update(String news);`

`}`

Next, let us create two concrete observers, each simulating a registered subscriber:

`public class MobileApp implements NewsObserver {`

`public void update(String news) {`

`System.out.println("Mobile App Alert: " + news);`

`}`

`}`

`public class WebsiteTicker implements NewsObserver {`

`public void update(String news) {`

`System.out.println("Website Ticker Update: " + news);`

`}`

`}`

Lastly, we need a program with a **`main()`** method so that we can run and test our application.

`public class ObserverExample {`

`public static void main(String[] args) {`

`BreakingNewsAgency agency = new BreakingNewsAgency();`

`NewsObserver mobile = new MobileApp();`

`NewsObserver web = new WebsiteTicker();`

`agency.subscribe(mobile);`

`agency.subscribe(web);`

`agency.notifySubscribers("Breaking: Championship Game Postponed!");`

`agency.unsubscribe(web);`

`agency.notifySubscribers("Update: New Airtime Announced for Game");`

`}`

`}`

Here is the output from this program:

`Mobile App Alert: Breaking: Championship Game Postponed!`

`Website Ticker Update: Breaking: Championship Game Postponed!`

`Mobile App Alert: Update: New Airtime Announced for Game`

# [Use Cases and Considerations](#toc.xhtml_s697a)

There are several instances when the use of this design pattern is appropriate, including the following:

*   Notification services
*   Event broadcasting systems
*   UI components with data hooks

The observer design pattern can be extremely beneficial to us and our systems. When implementing this pattern, we should consider that our system is more secure and easier to test due to the loose coupling between the subject and observers.

# [Strategy Pattern](#toc.xhtml_s698a)

The **strategy pattern** does the following:

1.  Defines a set of algorithms
2.  Encapsulates each algorithm
3.  Makes the algorithms interchangeable

This pattern ensures that changes can be made to the algorithms without affecting the clients/modules that rely on them.

We will design interchangeable algorithms using our television network’s feature that ranks trending programs. Different ranking algorithms may be used depending on the context such as:

*   Views per hour
*   User ratings
*   Social media mentions

Instead of hardcoding a single, clunky algorithm, we will define a strategy interface and switch strategies at runtime. Here is the interface:

`import java.util.List;`

`public interface RankingStrategy {`

`void rankPrograms(List<String> programs);`

`}`

Next, we will create two concrete strategies, each with a different rating context:

`import java.util.List;`

`public class ViewCountRanking implements RankingStrategy {`

`public void rankPrograms(List<String> programs) {`

`System.out.println("Ranking programs by hourly view count…");`

`// Placeholder logic`

`for (String program : programs) {`

`System.out.println(" - " + program);`

`}`

`}`

`}`

`import java.util.List;`

`public class SocialMediaRanking implements RankingStrategy {`

`public void rankPrograms(List<String> programs) {`

`System.out.println("Ranking programs by social media trends…");`

`for (String program : programs) {`

`System.out.println(" - " + program);`

`}`

`}`

`}`

Next, we need to create a concrete class:

`import java.util.List;`

`public class ProgramRanker {`

`private RankingStrategy strategy;`

`public void setStrategy(RankingStrategy strategy) {`

`this.strategy = strategy;`

`}`

`public void rank(List<String> programs) {`

`if (strategy != null) {`

`strategy.rankPrograms(programs);`

`} else {`

`System.out.println("No ranking strategy selected.");`

`}`

`}`

`}`

Lastly, we need a program with a **`main()`** method so we can run and test our application.

`import java.util.*;`

`public class StrategyExample {`

`public static void main(String[] args) {`

`List<String> programs = Arrays.asList("Evening News", "Drama Hour", "Sports Central");`

`ProgramRanker ranker = new ProgramRanker();`

`ranker.setStrategy(new ViewCountRanking());`

`ranker.rank(programs);`

`ranker.setStrategy(new SocialMediaRanking());`

`ranker.rank(programs);`

`}`

`}`

Here is the output from this program:

`Ranking programs by hourly view count…`

`- Evening News`

`- Drama Hour`

`- Sports Central`

`Ranking programs by social media trends…`

`- Evening News`

`- Drama Hour`

`- Sports Central`

# [Use Cases and Considerations](#toc.xhtml_s699a)

There are several instances when the use of this design pattern is appropriate, including the following:

*   When we need different algorithms to be swapped out, without having to modify the core logic.
*   When we want an alternative to lengthy **`switch`** and **`if-else`** statements.

The strategy design pattern can be extremely beneficial to us and our systems. When implementing this pattern, we should consider the concise and clean code that results.

# [Applying Design Patterns in Java Projects](#toc.xhtml_s700a)

We explored six specific design patterns and understanding their purpose and benefits is an important step. To truly realize their potential, we need to learn how to integrate multiple patterns and make smart trade-offs based on our project’s specific needs.

# [Integrating Multiple Patterns](#toc.xhtml_s701a)

Our study of design patterns was in isolation from other patterns, but we can implement multiple design patterns and have them work together. Remember, design patterns solve a problem, and our applications will have more than one problem to solve. For example, our TV network scenario might include a streaming platform that could use:

*   A Singleton for centralized logging
*   A Factory to instantiate different types of content providers
*   An Observer pattern to notify UI components of content updates
*   A Decorator to dynamically add a playback feature such as subtitles

The important aspect of using more than one design pattern is to know when and how they can complement each other. That can be done in layers, with each implemented pattern solving one component of a problem.

# [Trade-offs and Decision-making in Pattern Selection](#toc.xhtml_s702a)

Design patterns offer proven and reusable solutions to known problems. Each pattern has its own set of benefits and tradeoffs, and they should be carefully evaluated before implementing them. Here are some trade-offs to consider:

*   Design patterns often add layers of abstraction which might be unnecessary overhead for smaller applications.
*   Some design patterns could have a negative impact on performance such as with the decorator and strategy patterns that make additional method calls.
*   Design patterns often encapsulate details, making debugging and testing more difficult.

Making the right design pattern selection is important and requires a thorough evaluation of the current and future complexity of our application. We should strive to choose patterns that solve a real design problem, not just for the sake of using them. When possible, we should favor patterns that reduce coupling and increase application cohesion. Lastly, we should not hesitate to refactor our existing code to implement patterns as needed. While we might not always start with a design pattern, they can eventually be used as a better solution to a problem as our applications grow in scale.

# [Book Long Project](#toc.xhtml_s703a)

This section gives you the opportunity to improve your SLAP LMS application by applying key object-oriented design patterns. These patterns are not simply academic theory; rather, they are proven, practical strategies that solve real-world software architectural problems. By incorporating selected design patterns into your SLAP LMS, you can enhance its flexibility, maintainability, and scalability.

Your SLAP LMS can benefit from creational patterns to manage object creation consistently:

*   The singleton pattern can be used to centralize the management of system-wide resources, such as logging utilities or configuration services.
*   The factory pattern is ideal for dynamically creating different types of users (for example, student, instructor, administrator).

As your SLAP LMS grows, maintaining clean relationships between components becomes critical, and implementing structural design patterns can be helpful:

*   The adapter pattern can enable the LMS to integrate third-party systems such as external grading services or content providers, even if they use incompatible interfaces.
*   The decorator pattern can be used to add optional features (for example, time limits on quizzes, accessibility enhancements for course content) without modifying the original classes.

We can employ behavioral patterns to enhance how different parts of the LMS communicate and respond to change:

*   The observer pattern fits naturally into areas such as real-time updates. For example, students subscribed to a course can be automatically notified when new materials are added, or due dates are changed.
*   The strategy pattern can help us implement dynamic logic. For example, switching between different grading strategies or sorting methods for courses or users.

When the SLAP LMS is completed, it will be a large system, calling for the use of multiple design patterns. For example:

*   Use the factory pattern to instantiate different notification types.
*   Use the observer pattern to distribute those notifications.
*   Wrap notifications in a decorator to enhance them with different formatting or urgency levels.

This chapter’s principles can help transform your SLAP LMS from a functional system into a robust, architecturally sound system.

# [Conclusion](#toc.xhtml_s704a)

This chapter explored design patterns, characterizing them as powerful, reusable solutions to common software design problems. Understanding the featured design patterns, and considering their use during the software design process, shifts our minds from a pure software developer to that of a software architect.

We started with the purpose and value of design patterns and then examined two examples from each of the three major categories: creational, structural, and behavioral. Specifically, we looked at singleton and factory creational patterns that can help us manage object creation; the adapter and decorator structural patterns that help shape the relationships between objects; and the observer and strategy behavioral patterns that define how objects respond to changes.

The next chapter introduces the integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Java applications. You can learn how to use popular AI and machine learning libraries such as Deeplearning4j and Weka to build intelligent Java applications. The chapter covers various AI concepts, including machine learning, neural networks, and natural language processing. Specific topics include an introduction to AI and machine learning concepts, AI libraries, building machine learning models in Java, neural networks and deep learning with Java, natural language processing in Java, and practical AI applications in Java.

# [Points to Remember](#toc.xhtml_s705a)

*   Adapter pattern allows incompatible interfaces to work together without modifying their source code.
*   Behavioral patterns define how objects interact and delegate responsibilities during runtime.
*   Composition is preferred over inheritance in the decorator pattern to allow greater flexibility.
*   Creational patterns abstract the process of object creation to make systems more flexible.
*   Decorator pattern lets you add functionality to objects at runtime without altering their structure.
*   Design patterns provide reusable solutions to common software design problems in object-oriented programming.
*   Encapsulating algorithms using the strategy pattern allows behavior to change without modifying client code.
*   Factory pattern creates objects without specifying the exact class of the object to be created.
*   Factory method differs from simple factory in that it uses inheritance and relies on subclasses to instantiate objects.
*   Loose coupling is a benefit of many design patterns, including observer and strategy.
*   Observer pattern defines a one-to-many dependency so that when one object changes state, all dependents are notified.
*   Pattern synergy refers to the use of multiple design patterns working together to solve complex design problems.
*   Publish/subscribe systems are often implemented using the observer pattern to broadcast updates to multiple listeners.
*   Real-world Java applications often use multiple patterns in combination to manage creation, structure, and behavior.
*   Singleton pattern ensures that a class has only one instance and provides a global point of access to it.
*   Strategy pattern encapsulates a family of algorithms and makes them interchangeable.
*   Structural patterns focus on how classes and objects are composed to form larger systems.
*   Subscribers in the observer pattern register with a subject to receive automatic notifications when the state changes.
*   Trade-offs in pattern selection include balancing flexibility with complexity and maintainability with performance.
*   Using design patterns consistently can improve code readability, maintainability, and collaboration among developers.

# [Key Terms](#toc.xhtml_s709a)

*   **Adapter pattern:** A structural design pattern that allows incompatible interfaces to work together by acting as a translator.
*   **Behavioral patterns:** Design patterns that define how objects communicate and assign responsibilities during runtime.
*   **Creational patterns:** Design patterns focused on abstracting object instantiation.
*   **Decorator pattern:** A structural design pattern that allows additional behavior to be dynamically added to objects.
*   **Design patterns:** Reusable solutions to common problems in software design.
*   **Factory method:** A creational design pattern that delegates object creation to subclasses through an overridable method.
*   **Factory pattern:** A creational design pattern that centralizes and abstracts object creation.
*   **Loose coupling:** A desirable software design principle where components have minimal knowledge of each other.
*   **Observer pattern:** A behavioral design pattern where one object notifies multiple observers about state changes.
*   **Pattern synergy:** The practice of combining multiple design patterns to solve more complex architectural challenges.
*   **Simple factory:** A basic object creation approach where a method returns instances based on input parameters.
*   **Singleton pattern:** A creational design pattern that ensures a class has only one instance accessible globally.
*   **Strategy pattern:** A behavioral design pattern that defines a group of algorithms and makes them interchangeable.
*   **Structural patterns:** Design patterns concerned with the relationships between components.

# [Exercises](#toc.xhtml_s710a)

**Exercise 1: Implementing a Singleton Logger**

**Objective**: Reinforce understanding of the singleton design pattern through practical application.

**Activity**: Create a Logger class that uses the singleton pattern to ensure only one instance exists. The logger should provide a method **`log(String message)`** that prints the message to the console, prefixed with a timestamp. Write a **`main()`** method to simulate multiple components of an application writing log messages and confirm that the logger instance is the same across all calls.

**Exercise 2: TV Program Factory**

**Objective**: Practice implementing the Factory pattern with a focus on flexible object creation.

**Activity**: Perform the following actions:

*   Define an interface **`TVProgram`** and create at least three concrete classes (for example, **`NewsProgram`**, **`ComedyShow`**, **`Documentary`**).
*   Then, implement a **`TVProgramFactory`** class with a method **`createProgram(String type)`** that returns the appropriate program instance.
*   Write a test class to create different programs based on user input or test cases and call a **`play()`** method on each.

**Exercise 3: Integrating an External Weather Service using an Adapter**

**Objective**: Apply the adapter pattern to integrate incompatible interfaces.

**Activity**: Perform the following actions:

*   Simulate an external class T**`hirdPartyWeatherAPI`** with a method **`getForecast()`**.
*   Create an internal interface **`WeatherService`** with a method **`fetchWeather()`**.
*   Implement an adapter class that allows the external API to work with your internal interface.
*   Write a program that uses the adapter to display the forecast using your internal interface.

**Exercise 4: Adding Features with Decorators**

**Objective**: Demonstrate the use of the Decorator pattern to dynamically add behavior.

**Activity**: Perform the following actions:

*   Implement a base class **`BasicProgram`** that displays a program title.
*   Then, create decorators such as **`CaptionedProgram`** and **`AdSupportedProgram`** that extend functionality.
*   Write a program that wraps a **`BasicProgram`** with multiple decorators and displays the final output to show layered behavior (for example, “Now playing: Science Show [Captions On] [Ads Enabled]”).

**Exercise 5: Ranking System with the Strategy Pattern**

**Objective**: Use the strategy pattern to switch between different algorithms at runtime.

**Activity**: Perform the following actions:

*   Define a **`RankingStrategy`** interface with a method **`rank(List<String> programs)`**.
*   Implement at least two strategies: one that ranks alphabetically and one that ranks by simulated popularity score.
*   Create a **`ProgramRanker`** class that can accept a ranking strategy and apply it.
*   Write a **`main()`** method to demonstrate switching strategies on the same list of programs.

# [Using AI with Java Programming](#toc.xhtml_c19)

# [Introduction](#toc.xhtml_s711a)

This chapter introduces foundational concepts of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML), and how to integrate those technologies into Java projects. You will have the opportunity to learn how to work with Java-compatible AI libraries such as Deeplearning4j and Weka. The hands-on examples and practical exercises featured in this chapter can provide insight into how to train models, evaluate their performance, and use them to solve real-world problems. Natural Language Processing (NLP) will also be introduced.

By the end of this chapter, you should have a solid understanding of the core concepts of artificial intelligence and machine learning. This includes relevance to modern software development. You should be able to identify and utilize Java-compatible AI libraries and understand their strengths and use cases. By the chapter’s end, you should be able to build and train machine learning models in Java, as well as implement simple neural networks and deep learning solutions. Additionally, you should understand how to apply natural language processing (NLP) techniques in Java. Finally, by the end of this chapter, you should be able to develop a basic AI-powered Java application that demonstrates real-world functionality.

# [Structure](#toc.xhtml_s712a)

In this chapter, the following topics will be covered:

*   Introduction to AI and Machine Learning Concepts
*   Integrating Java with AI Libraries
*   Building Machine Learning Models in Java
*   Neural Networks and Deep Learning with Java
*   Natural Language Processing in Java
*   Practical AI Applications in Java

# [Introduction to AI and Machine Learning Concepts](#toc.xhtml_s713a)

The term Artificial Intelligence (AI) has become ubiquitous in recent years. AI is the simulation of human intelligence. It resides in machines and is capable of learning, reasoning, problem-solving, and adapting to changes in its environment and new information. Machine Learning (ML) is part of AI and, as the name suggests, focuses on enabling systems to learn from data. Instead of relying on a series of hardcoded rules, ML uses statistical methods to identify patterns and make decisions.

To enable machine learning, we use a dataset to train a model. We evaluate the model’s performance and then use it to make predictions on new data. There are three primary categories of how machines learn (supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement). Together, they form the foundation of modern AI. Let us look at each of these types of learning.

# [Supervised Learning](#toc.xhtml_s714a)

**Supervised learning**, the most common type of machine learning, involves our use of a labeled dataset to train a model. This is a straightforward approach where each input has a correct output. Our goal with supervised learning is to teach the model the relationship between inputs and outputs. Once learned, the model will be able to predict outcomes for new data.

Common use cases for supervised learning include classification (for example, spam detection and sentiment analysis) and regression (for example, predicting housing prices and weather).

# [Unsupervised Learning](#toc.xhtml_s715a)

A second type of learning in machine learning is **unsupervised learning**. The dataset used for training a model is not labeled. Our goal with this type of learning is to discover hidden patterns or groupings within the data. There are advanced algorithms (for example, clustering and dimensionality reduction used with this type of learning.

Common use cases for unsupervised learning include anomaly detection and customer segmentation.

# [Reinforcement Learning](#toc.xhtml_s716a)

The third category of learning for machine learning is **reinforcement learning.** This is the most complex form of machine learning. In this approach, a model learns to make decisions by interacting with its environment. The model receives reward or penalty feedback, adjusting its actions to maximize rewards. This type of learning is not typically implemented with Java programming and is included here to fully cover the topic.

Common use cases of reinforcement learning include autonomous systems, game AI, and robotics.

# [Integrating Java with AI Libraries](#toc.xhtml_s717a)

We cannot create powerful AI applications with Java’s core libraries alone. We need to leverage libraries that simplify machine learning. This section highlights the two most used Java-compatible libraries (Deeplearning4j and Weka). These libraries are used for different purposes. Let us look at each of them next.

# [Deeplearning4j](#toc.xhtml_s718a)

The **Deeplearning4j** library is open-source and is commonly used with Java and the Java Virtual Machine (JVM). It has the singular purpose of building and training deep neural networks. This makes it ideally suited for complex tasks to include the following:

*   Image recognition
*   Video recognition
*   Natural language processing
*   Fraud detection
*   Sentiment analysis
*   Predictive analysis
*   Time-series analysis

Deeplearning4j supports **Graphic Processing Unit** (**GPU**) acceleration via **Compute Unified Device Architecture** (**CUDA**) to support the computing load and faster model training. It also integrates with **N-Dimensional Arrays for Java** (**ND4J**), which is a scientific computing library.

This library can be used for building deep learning architectures to include Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), Long Short-Term Memory Networks (LSTMs), and Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs). The Deeplearning4j library is suitable for enterprise-level applications.

# [Setup Instructions](#toc.xhtml_s719a)

To set up Deeplearning4j, you will first need to download the latest JARs from the official GitHub page: **`https://github.com/deeplearning4j/deeplearning4j`**

You will need, at a minimum, the following:

*   deeplearning4j-core
*   nd4j-native-platform

As with other libraries, you should add the JARs to your project’s **`lib/`** folder.

For a great starting guide to Deeplearning4j, you can visit the site listed below:

**`https://www.baeldung.com/deeplearning4j`**

# [Weka](#toc.xhtml_s720a)

Our second featured library is the **Waikato Environment for Knowledge Analysis** (Weka). This library is suitable for traditional machine learning with tools to support the following:

*   Classification
*   Clustering
*   Data preprocessing
*   Regression
*   Visualization

This library includes a graphical user interface and Java API, making it easy to learn. Weka requires minimal code and supports classic machine learning algorithms such as decision trees, k-nearest neighbors, and Naïve Bayes. Common use cases include:

*   Machine learning prototyping
*   Educational purposes
*   Classification of structured/tabular data
*   Exploratory data analysis
*   Rapid experimentation and testing of algorithms

# [Setup Instructions](#toc.xhtml_s721a)

To setup Weka, follow these steps:

1.  Download the standalone JAR file from the official Weka website: **`https://www.weka.io/`** or here: **`https://ml.cms.waikato.ac.nz/weka/`**
2.  Add the JAR to your project’s **`lib/`** folder.
3.  Add the JAR to your classpath
4.  Verify setup with a simple Java program such as this:

    `import weka.classifiers.trees.J48;`

    `import weka.core.Instances;`

    `import weka.core.converters.ConverterUtils.DataSource;`

    `public class WekaTest {`

    `public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {`

    `DataSource source = new DataSource("data.arff");`

    `Instances data = source.getDataSet();`

    `data.setClassIndex(data.numAttributes() - 1);`

    `J48 tree = new J48(); // decision tree`

    `tree.buildClassifier(data);`

    `System.out.println(tree);`

    `}`

    `}`

# [Building Machine Learning Modules in Java](#toc.xhtml_s722a)

This section demonstrates building a machine learning module in Java. We will walk through a classification example using Weka that loads a dataset, trains a decision tree classifier (J48, Weka’s implementation of the C4.5 algorithm), evaluates the model, and prints the results.

1.  If you have not already downloaded Weka, refer to the previous section
2.  Move the Weka **`.jar`** file into your project’s **`lib/`** folder.
3.  Add your **`.jar`** file to your classpath. Add a **`.vscode/settings.json`** file in your project with the following content:

    `{`

    `"java.project.referencedLibraries": [`

    `"lib/weka.jar"`

    `]`

    `}`

4.  Next, we need a dataset. For this example, we will use the often-used Iris dataset. We will create an **`iris.arff`** file (Attribute-Relation File Format) with the following content:

    `@relation iris`

    `@attribute sepallength numeric`

    `@attribute sepalwidth numeric`

    `@attribute petallength numeric`

    `@attribute petalwidth numeric`

    `@attribute class {Iris-setosa,Iris-versicolor,Iris-virginica}`

    `@data`

    `5.1,3.5,1.4,0.2,Iris-setosa`

    `4.9,3.0,1.4,0.2,Iris-setosa`

    `6.2,2.8,4.8,1.8,Iris-versicolor`

    `5.9,3.0,5.1,1.8,Iris-virginica`

5.  Now, we need to write a classifier class. Here is one named **`IrisClassifier.java`**:

    `import weka.classifiers.Classifier;`

    `import weka.classifiers.trees.J48;`

    `import weka.core.Instances;`

    `import weka.core.converters.ConverterUtils.DataSource;`

    `import weka.classifiers.Evaluation;`

    `public class IrisClassifier {`

    `public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {`

    `// Load dataset`

    `DataSource source = new DataSource("iris.arff");`

    `Instances data = source.getDataSet();`

    `// Set class index to the last attribute (the target class)`

    `data.setClassIndex(data.numAttributes() - 1);`

    `// Initialize the classifier (J48 Decision Tree)`

    `Classifier classifier = new J48();`

    `classifier.buildClassifier(data);`

    `// Instead of cross-validation:`

    `Evaluation eval = new Evaluation(data);`

    `eval.evaluateModel(classifier, data);`

    `// Output model and evaluation metrics`

    `System.out.println(classifier);`

    `System.out.println(eval.toSummaryString("\n=== Evaluation Results ===\n", false));`

    `System.out.println("Confusion Matrix:");`

    `double[][] matrix = eval.confusionMatrix();`

    `for (double[] row : matrix) {`

    `for (double val : row) {`

    `System.out.print((int) val + " ");`

    `}`

    `System.out.println();`

    `}`

    `}`

    `}`

6.  Now, we compile our program with the following command:

    `javac -cp ".:lib/weka.jar" IrisClassifier.java`

7.  Lastly, we can run our program:

    `java --add-opens java.base/java.lang=ALL-UNNAMED -cp ".:lib/weka.jar" IrisClassifier`

    Our code’s output follows (some blank lines were removed for brevity):

    `J48 pruned tree`

    `------------------`

    `sepallength <= 5.1: Iris-setosa (2.0)`

    `sepallength > 5.1: Iris-versicolor (2.0/1.0)`

    `Number of Leaves  :     2`

    `Size of the tree :      3`

    `=== Evaluation Results ===`

    `Correctly Classified Instances           3               75      %`

    `Incorrectly Classified Instances         1               25      %`

    `Kappa statistic                          0.6  `

    `Mean absolute error                      0.1667`

    `Root mean squared error                  0.2887`

    `Relative absolute error                 38.8889 %`

    `Root relative squared error             62.8619 %`

    `Total Number of Instances                4`

    `Confusion Matrix:`

    `2 0 0`

    `0 1 0`

    `0 1 0`

Exploring our code’s output, we can confirm that the decision tree structure was printed to the console. The evaluation results include metrics such as accuracy and error rate and the confusion matrix shows how well the classifier predicted each class.

This simple example demonstrates the workflow of building and evaluating a machine learning model in Java.

# [Neural Networks and Deep Learning in Java](#toc.xhtml_s723a)

Neural networks are created to identify complex data patterns for applications such as natural language processing, predictive analytics, and image recognition. These networks are inspired by and modeled by the workings of the human brain and how it processes data. These networks consist of cooperative layers. We use deep learning, a specialized component of machine learning, to create and train these models.

Follow the steps below to learn how to build a basic neural network from scratch.

1.  Obtain the required JAR files from this site:
    1.  [https://github.com/deeplearning4j/deeplearning4j](https://github.com/deeplearning4j/deeplearning4j)
2.  Place the JAR files listed below in your project’s **`lib/`** folder.
    1.  `deeplearning4j-core`
    2.  `nd4j-native-platform`
    3.  `datavec-api`
3.  Create a **`settings.json`** file in your project’s **`.vscode/`** folder

    `{`

    `"java.project.referencedLibraries": [`

    `"lib/**/*.jar"`

    `]`

    `}`

4.  Now we are ready to create a neural network. We will use a simple XOR data set to show how a neural network can learn basic logic operations.

    `import org.nd4j.linalg.api.ndarray.INDArray;`

    `import org.nd4j.linalg.factory.Nd4j;`

    `import org.nd4j.linalg.dataset.DataSet;`

    `import org.deeplearning4j.nn.multilayer.MultiLayerNetwork;`

    `import org.deeplearning4j.nn.conf.MultiLayerConfiguration;`

    `import org.deeplearning4j.nn.conf.NeuralNetConfiguration;`

    `import org.deeplearning4j.nn.conf.layers.DenseLayer;`

    `import org.deeplearning4j.nn.conf.layers.OutputLayer;`

    `import org.nd4j.linalg.lossfunctions.LossFunctions;`

    `import org.nd4j.linalg.activations.Activation;`

    `import org.nd4j.linalg.learning.config.Sgd;`

    `public class SimpleXORModel {`

    `public static void main(String[] args) {`

    `// Define XOR input and output`

    `INDArray input = Nd4j.create(new double[][] {`

    `{0, 0},`

    `{0, 1},`

    `{1, 0},`

    `{1, 1}`

    `});`

    `INDArray labels = Nd4j.create(new double[][] {`

    `{0},`

    `{1},`

    `{1},`

    `{0}`

    `});`

    `// Create dataset`

    `DataSet ds = new DataSet(input, labels);`

    `// Configure the neural network`

    `MultiLayerConfiguration config = new NeuralNetConfiguration.Builder()`

    `.seed(123)`

    `.updater(new Sgd(0.1))`

    `.list()`

    `.layer(new DenseLayer.Builder()`

    `.nIn(2)`

    `.nOut(4)`

    `.activation(Activation.SIGMOID)`

    `.build())`

    `.layer(new OutputLayer.Builder()`

    `.nIn(4)`

    `.nOut(1)`

    `.activation(Activation.SIGMOID)`

    `.lossFunction(LossFunctions.LossFunction.MSE)`

    `.build())`

    `.build();`

    `MultiLayerNetwork model = new MultiLayerNetwork(config);`

    `model.init();`

    `// Train the model`

    `for (int i = 0; i < 10000; i++) {`

    `model.fit(ds);`

    `}`

    `// Test the model`

    `INDArray output = model.output(input);`

    `System.out.println("Input:\n" + input);`

    `System.out.println("Predicted Output:\n" + output);`

    `}`

    `}`

5.  You can now compile and run your application with the following commands:

    `javac -cp ".:lib/*" SimpleXORModel.java`

    `java -cp ".:lib/*" SimpleXORModel`

    Our program’s output is provided below:

    `SLF4J: Failed to load class "org.slf4j.impl.StaticLoggerBinder".`

    `SLF4J: Defaulting to no-operation (NOP) logger implementation`

    `SLF4J: See http://www.slf4j.org/codes.html#StaticLoggerBinder for further details.`

    `Input:`

    `[[         0,         0],`

    `[         0,    1.0000],`

    `[    1.0000,         0],`

    `[    1.0000,    1.0000]]`

    `Predicted Output:`

    `[[0.4860],`

    `[0.5393],`

    `[0.5073],`

    `[0.4444]]`

You will note that the output started with three **`SLF4J`** messages. Deeplearning4j and ND4J are trying to use **`SLF4J`** for logging. We do not have a backend logging schema setup, so you can ignore those messages.

If you have any difficulties, you can use the **`SimpleXORMaven`** package that is bundled with this chapter’s source code.

# [Natural Language Processing in Java](#toc.xhtml_s724a)

**Natural Language Processing** (**NLP**), like machine learning, is a subset of artificial intelligence. This technology helps computers understand, analyze, and even generate human language. In today’s technologically advanced society, this technology is in use as chatbots, virtual assistants, user interfaces, and more.

There are several tools available to us in Java that support NLP. This includes **Weka**, which was covered earlier in this chapter. Additional tools include the **Stanford CoreNLP** and **Apache Open NLP**. This section reviews each of those tools.

# [Weka](#toc.xhtml_s725a)

NLP is not Weka’s greatest strength, it is primarily used for classification, clustering, and regression; however, it does have support for basic text mining and NLP tasks. Specifically, Weka includes a **`StringToWordVector`** filter that can convert text data into numerical feature vectors. This is an approach to train machine learning models on text.

Weka is just an honorable mention here due to its lack of advanced linguistic processing capabilities (that is, tokenization, tagging, and so on). Additionally, there are not a lot of NLP libraries or tools for Java.

# [Stanford CoreNLP](#toc.xhtml_s726a)

**Stanford CoreNLP** is a Java-based NLP library that supports linguistic annotations including:

*   Coreference resolution
*   Dependency parsing
*   Lemmatization
*   Named entity recognition (NER)
*   Part-of-speech (POS) tagging
*   Sentence splitting
*   Sentiment analysis
*   Tokenization

CoreNLP is available to us via a command-line interface and a Java API. This tool is frequently used for advanced NLP pipelines and analyzing text documents.

Here is a code snippet using CoreNLP:

`Properties props = new Properties();`

`props.setProperty("annotators", "tokenize,ssplit,pos,lemma,ner");`

`StanfordCoreNLP pipeline = new StanfordCoreNLP(props);`

`CoreDocument doc = new CoreDocument("Jimmy went to Tennessee last week.");`

`pipeline.annotate(doc);`

`for (CoreEntityMention em : doc.entityMentions()) {`

`System.out.println(em.text() + " -> " + em.entityType());`

`}`

# [Apache OpenNLP](#toc.xhtml_s727a)

**Apache OpenNLP** is our third NLP library that can be used with Java. It supports the following functions:

*   Chunking
*   Document classification
*   Named entity recognition
*   Parsing
*   POS tagging
*   Sentence detection
*   Tokenization

OpenNLP includes pre-trained models for multiple languages. It is designed for real-time NLP applications. This is a lightweight tool suited for practical applications, emphasizing speed and simplicity.

The code snippet below uses OpenNLP for sentence detection:

`InputStream modelIn = new FileInputStream("en-sent.bin");`

`SentenceModel model = new SentenceModel(modelIn);`

`SentenceDetectorME detector = new SentenceDetectorME(model);`

`String[] sentences = detector.sentDetect("Program everyday.` `Practice NLP with Java.");`

`for (String sentence : sentences) {`

`System.out.println(sentence);`

`}`

# [Practical AI Applications with Java](#toc.xhtml_s728a)

Programming robust AI applications is beyond the scope of this chapter, but it is nonetheless important to consider Java for your future AI-related applications. This section explores four example AI-related projects, each highlighting a real-world AI application. Instead of providing lengthy implementations, this section provides a high-level overview of each application’s purpose, the technologies required, and an approach to the project.

# [Email Spam Classifier](#toc.xhtml_s729a)

An email spam classifier would be categorized as a text classifier. Creating this system would require machine learning and natural language processing. Appropriate libraries are Weka or Apache OpenNLP. This project would have the purpose of classifying emails as spam or not spam based on the email’s content. Key to this implementation would be a dataset consisting of labeled emails, keywords, and potentially word frequency.

Dependencies could include:

*   weka-stable.jar for classification and preprocessing
*   opennlp-tools.jar for tokenization and sentence splitting

Here is a suggested methodology:

1.  Convert email content into numeric features using Weka’s **`StringToWordVector`** filter
2.  Train a classification model
3.  Evaluate model accuracy using cross-validation
4.  Allow users to input new messages and receive real-time classification

# [Loan Approval Predictor](#toc.xhtml_s730a)

Many financial institutions undoubtedly employ AI tools to provide predictive analytics to include loan approval predictions. The Weka library is ideally suited for this type of application. Imagine that a bank or financial institution wants to automate loan application assessments based on applicant data such as income, credit score, employment history, and debt-to-income ratio. This is something we could easily develop a model for.

Dependencies could include Weka for dataset preprocessing and classification.

Here is a suggested methodology:

1.  Use a historical dataset of loan approvals and rejections
2.  Preprocess the data
    1.  Handle missing values
    2.  Normalize numerical features
3.  Train a decision tree or logistic regression model
4.  Evaluate results and use the model to predict outcomes for new applications

# [Sentiment Analyzer](#toc.xhtml_s731a)

A sentiment analyzer for product reviews would be an application that employs both NLP and text classification. We could use the Stanford CoreNLP or Apache OpenNLP library for this project. Depending on the finite requirements, we might also use Deeplearning4j. This application would identify whether product reviews are positive, negative, or neutral. It might be a standalone application, embedded on a web page, or part of a larger e-commerce system.

Dependencies could include:

*   Stanford CoreNLP for tokenization, lemmatization, and sentiment analysis
*   Deeplearning4j if training a custom sentiment model

Here is a suggested methodology:

1.  Use CoreNLP’s pretrained sentiment model to analyze review text
2.  Fine-tune our own model using labeled datasets
3.  Output sentiment scores or labels for each review

# [AI-powered Chat Assistant](#toc.xhtml_s732a)

Our final featured AI-related project is a basic AI-powered chat assistant. This application would belong to the domains of machine learning and natural language processing. The most applicable library would be Apache OpenNLP. Our project would be a lightweight, rule-driven chatbot. We would give our chatbot the capability of answering common user queries. This simple example is prevalent across customer service portals.

Dependencies could include Apache OpenNLP for sentence detection, tokenization, and named entity recognition.

Here is a suggested methodology:

1.  Define a set of common intents and responses
2.  Use OpenNLP to process user input and extract keywords or entities
3.  Match input patterns to known responses using basic rules or classifiers
4.  Return pre-written or dynamically generated responses

# [Book Long Project](#toc.xhtml_s733a)

As you think about this chapter’s content in the context of your SLAP LMS, consider how your application’s users could benefit from integrating AI technologies. This section does not propose that you redesign your LMS or embed full-scale AI models, but rather conceptualize enhancements that you could implement in your system’s future iterations.

Here is a list of possible AI enhancements for your SLAP LMS:

*   Using supervised machine learning, the SLAP LMS could analyze student behavior (for example, time spent on materials, quiz performance, and course progression) to recommend:
    *   Courses they might enjoy or benefit from
    *   Supplementary readings or exercises
    *   Suggested timelines based on learning speed
*   A lightweight AI-powered chatbot could provide students with real-time answers to frequently asked questions such as:
    *   “How do I reset my password?”
    *   “What are my upcoming assignments?”
    *   “When is the next live lecture?”
*   Course evaluations could be scanned to detect overall student sentiment. This could help instructors Tailor their interactions with students. The system could tag sentiment scores (positive, neutral, negative) and provide visual summaries to course administrators.
*   SLAP LMS could implement a basic document similarity checker using vector space models and text classification:
    *   Compare student-submitted assignments using Weka’s text preprocessing tools.
    *   Flag potentially copied content for manual review.
*   You could implement predictive analytics for student success by combining historical performance data and demographic variables. The LMS could then:
    *   Predict students at risk of falling behind
    *   Trigger early alerts to instructors or support staff
*   An intelligent engine could assess a student’s past performance and dynamically select quiz questions based on their ability level:
    *   Easy questions for struggling learners
    *   Challenging items for those performing well
    *   Future iterations could use reinforcement learning strategies for adaptive assessment mechanisms.
*   Rather than sending uniform notifications, the LMS could prioritize or personalize them:
    *   Highlight overdue tasks with urgency
    *   Suggest focused study sessions based on habits

# [Design Considerations](#toc.xhtml_s734a)

Incorporating AI functionality in your SLAP LMS should be done with the following considerations:

*   You should take care to use AI responsibly. For example, predictions should support students, not penalize them.
*   Provide students and faculty with insight into how and why certain recommendations are made.
*   Ensure that all data used for AI models complies with privacy policies and regulations.

# [Points to Remember](#toc.xhtml_s736a)

*   Apache OpenNLP is a library that supports tasks such as tokenization, sentence detection, and named entity recognition.
*   Deeplearning4j is a deep learning framework suitable for building and training neural networks.
*   Java-compatible libraries such as Weka and Deeplearning4j make it possible to develop machine learning and AI applications without switching to other programming languages.
*   Machine learning enables systems to learn from data rather than relying on hardcoded rules or logic.
*   Model training involves feeding labeled data to an algorithm so it can learn patterns and make predictions on unseen data.
*   Natural Language Processing (NLP) involves techniques that allow computers to understand, interpret, and respond to human language.
*   Neural networks consist of layers of interconnected nodes that adjust weights during training to learn complex patterns.
*   OpenNLP provides pre-trained models for multiple languages and supports both rule-based and statistical NLP methods.
*   Sentiment analysis is an NLP task that determines whether a piece of text expresses a positive, negative, or neutral opinion.
*   Stanford CoreNLP is a comprehensive suite of NLP tools that supports tokenization, part-of-speech tagging, lemmatization, parsing, and sentiment analysis.
*   Supervised learning uses labeled data to train a model that can make predictions based on new input.
*   Training data is a set of input-output pairs used to teach a machine learning model how to make predictions.
*   Unsupervised learning analyzes data without labeled outputs and is used for tasks such as clustering and dimensionality reduction.
*   Weka is a GUI-based and programmatic Java machine learning library that supports data preprocessing, classification, clustering, regression, and visualization.
*   XOR classification is a common introductory task for neural networks and requires non-linear models due to its non-separable nature.

# [Key Terms](#toc.xhtml_s740a)

*   **Artificial Intelligence (AI):** The simulation of human intelligence processes by machines.
*   **Apache OpenNLP:** A Java-based library used for natural language processing tasks.
*   **Classification:** A supervised learning task in which input data is categorized into predefined labels or groups.
*   **Confusion Matrix:** A table used to evaluate the performance of a classification model by comparing predicted labels with actual labels.
*   **Cross-Validation:** A technique used to assess how well a model generalizes to unseen data by partitioning the dataset into training and validation sets.
*   **Data Preprocessing:** The steps taken to clean, normalize, and prepare raw data for machine learning or AI applications.
*   **DataSet:** A structure used in Deeplearning4j that holds input and output data for training a model.
*   **Deeplearning4j (DL4J):** A Java-based deep learning library that allows the creation and training of neural networks.
*   **Feedforward Neural Network:** A type of artificial neural network where connections between the nodes do not form cycles.
*   **Labeled Data:** Data that includes both input features and corresponding correct output values used in supervised learning.
*   **Machine Learning (ML):** A subfield of AI focused on building systems that can learn from data and make decisions without being explicitly programmed.
*   **Natural Language Processing (NLP):** A field of AI that focuses on enabling computers to interpret and process human language.
*   **ND4J:** A scientific computing library used in conjunction with Deeplearning4j for high-performance numerical operations.
*   **Neural Network:** A network of interconnected nodes designed to recognize patterns and perform tasks such as classification or prediction.
*   **Prediction:** The output generated by a trained machine learning model when applied to new or unseen data.
*   **Supervised Learning:** A type of machine learning that uses labeled data to train models to make accurate predictions.
*   **Tokenizer:** A component in NLP that splits text into individual tokens such as words or punctuation marks.
*   **Training Data:** The portion of a dataset used to teach a machine learning model how to make predictions.
*   **Unsupervised Learning:** A type of machine learning where the algorithm learns from data without labeled outputs.
*   **Weka:** A Java-based machine learning toolkit that supports data preprocessing, classification, regression, clustering, and visualization.
*   **XOR Problem:** A fundamental logic problem used to demonstrate the capabilities of neural networks that require non-linear solutions.

# [Exercises](#toc.xhtml_s741a)

**Exercise 1: Build a Simple Text Classifier**

**Objective:** Learn how to preprocess text and build a supervised machine learning model using Weka.

**Activity:** Prepare a small dataset of product reviews labeled as positive or negative. Convert the data into ARFF format and use Weka’s **`StringToWordVector`** filter to transform the text. Train a **`Naive Bayes`** classifier and evaluate its performance using 10-fold cross-validation. Submit your ARFF file and a brief summary of the classifier’s accuracy and confusion matrix.

**Exercise 2: Train a Neural Network**

**Objective:** Gain experience configuring and training a basic neural network using Deeplearning4j.

**Activity:** Implement a feedforward neural network in Java using Deeplearning4j to solve the XOR logic problem. Configure the network with one hidden layer and train it on the four possible input-output combinations. Display the model’s predicted outputs after training. Submit your Java code and a screenshot of the results.

**Exercise 3: Explore NLP with Apache OpenNLP**

**Objective:** Apply sentence detection and tokenization techniques to real-world text.

**Activity:** Download and use the Apache OpenNLP library to create a Java program that takes a paragraph of user input and outputs the tokenized words and detected sentences. Use the pre-trained models provided with OpenNLP. Submit your Java code and output from a sample text of your choice.

**Exercise 4: Compare Supervised and Unsupervised Learning Models**

**Objective:** Understand the differences between supervised and unsupervised learning in practice.

**Activity:** Use Weka to load a dataset that includes both numeric attributes and class labels. Train a supervised model and an unsupervised model. Compare the results and describe how each model interpreted the data. Submit a short explanation and screenshots of your Weka output.

**Exercise 5: Evaluate Sentiment**

**Objective:** Use a pre-built sentiment analysis tool to process and interpret user-generated text.

**Activity:** Install Stanford CoreNLP and use it in a Java program to evaluate the sentiment of at least five product or movie reviews. Print the detected sentiment for each review. Submit your code along with the original text and the sentiment results.
