# [Introduction](#toc.xhtml_s742a)

This chapter brings together everything the earlier chapters covered. This project-based chapter will combine the concepts and techniques you gained exposure to throughout this book into a complete Java application from the ground up.

Our final project is a desktop-based task management application called TaskWise AI. This application will allow users to add and manage tasks with a simple JavaFX interface, store those tasks in a local SQLite database, and apply a basic AI feature to automatically suggest task priorities based on the task description. We will begin by planning and designing the application, then progressively build and test it, applying the techniques covered throughout this book.

This chapter is designed to reinforce your skills in a practical, complete application. You can gain valuable experience working through a real-world development workflow, from project design and dependency setup to implementation and final testing.

By the end of this chapter, you should be able to design a complete Java application, install and verify required libraries, build a JavaFX user interface for desktop application, and implement persistent data storage. Furthermore, you will be able to incorporate a basic AI logic module, apply exception handling, and understand how to approach testing and optimization.

# [Structure](#toc.xhtml_s743a)

In this chapter, the following topics will be covered:

*   Final Project
*   Next Steps

# [Final Project](#toc.xhtml_s744a)

In this section, we will review a set of requirements, design an application to those requirements, set up a project and its dependencies in VS Code, implement the core functionality, finalize, and test our Java application. We will build a complete desktop application, called TaskWise AI. It will be an intelligent task organizer designed to help users effectively manage their to-do lists. This project provides you with a practical, hands-on opportunity to integrate key programming concepts presented throughout this book into a single, cohesive application.

# [Project Requirements](#toc.xhtml_s745a)

Our application, TaskWise AI will be a lightweight Java-based task management tool. Its key feature is the ability to analyze task descriptions and automatically suggest a priority level using basic AI logic. Our goal is to create a useful, user-friendly productivity app while reinforcing our knowledge of object-oriented programming, graphical user interfaces, data persistence, and lightweight AI.

The application will allow users to perform the following actions:

*   Add, edit, and delete tasks using a simple and intuitive form
*   Display tasks in a table that supports dynamic updates
*   Filter or sort tasks based on date or status
*   Apply AI-based suggestions that automatically assign a priority level based on keywords detected in the task description

The project’s scope is designed to provide a simple, yet realistic example of how modern desktop applications can be built.

# [Core Components](#toc.xhtml_s746a)

To complete this project, we will utilize the following Java components and libraries:

*   JavaFX for a graphical user interface (GUI)
*   SQLite for data storage and persistence
*   Simple AI logic
*   Java input/output logging
*   Exception handling
*   Object-oriented programming
*   Collections

# [Application Design](#toc.xhtml_s747a)

Before we set up and program our application, we need to consider its design. It is important that our TaskWise AI application be well-organized, scalable, and maintainable. This section walks through a proposed class structure, use cases, and functional requirements that will guide the development of this project.

# [Class Diagram and Design](#toc.xhtml_s748a)

TaskWise AI will be composed of several key classes, each with a focused responsibility to promote separation of concerns and ease of maintenance. *[Figure 20.1](#c20.xhtml_fig20_1)* illustrates the planned classes that form the core architecture of our application.

![](images/Figure-20.1.jpg)

**Figure 20.1:** TaskWise AI Application Class Diagram

Referring to *[Figure 20.1](#c20.xhtml_fig20_1)*, here is a description of the key classes planned for our TaskWise AI application:

*   **Task:** This class represents a single task with fields such as id, title, description, dueDate, status, and priority.
*   **TaskManager:** This will be our controller class responsible for managing the in-memory list of tasks. It will provide methods to add, remove, update, and retrieve tasks. It will be the bridge between the GUI and the database.
*   **DatabaseHelper:** This class will handle all interactions with our SQLite database, including creating tables, saving and loading tasks, and executing SQL queries.
*   **AIAnalyzer:** This class will provide a simple logic engine to analyze task descriptions and suggest a priority level. It will search for keywords in the text and return a recommended priority.
*   **MainApp:** As the name suggests, this will be our application’s entry point. It will initialize the GUI and manage the JavaFX stage, scene, and event handling.
*   **DependenciesChecker:** This will be a utility class created to verify the required libraries (for example, JavaFX, SQLite JDBC) are available to our application. We will use it to provide confirmation messages or error notifications to the console.

Together, these classes will form the core architecture of our application.

# [Use Cases](#toc.xhtml_s749a)

Reviewing use cases will help us fully understand the TaskWise AI application. Here are the main operations users will perform in the application:

*   **Create a new task:** Users can input task details (title, description, due date) and add them to the task list.
*   **View tasks:** All existing tasks are displayed in a JavaFX table. Users can scroll through and review their to-do items.
*   **Edit or delete tasks:** Users can select a task from the table and either update its details or remove it from the list.
*   **Run AI suggestion:** With a click of a button, users can trigger the AI analyzer to suggest a priority level based on the task description.
*   **Exit and save:** When exiting the application, users’ tasks are saved to the SQLite database for persistence across sessions.

These use cases form the foundation of the application’s features and user interaction flow.

# [Functional Requirements](#toc.xhtml_s750a)

Designing and developing a complete desktop Java application with a GUI, database functionality, and an AI component can be complex so we need to limit it so the project can be completed in this chapter. To that end, the following functional requirements are established:

*   **No network access:** All data and logic will be handled locally. The application will be self-contained and not require an internet connection.
*   **Offline storage and execution:** The application uses a local SQLite database to persist user data between sessions. This enables offline use without any remote dependencies.
*   **User-friendly GUI:** The interface is built using JavaFX and designed for simplicity and ease of use. The GUI will consist of task input fields, action buttons, and table views arranged to support intuitive task management without the need for training or instructions.

Now that our application has been fully designed and scoped, we are ready to set up our project in Visual Studio Code.

# [Project Setup](#toc.xhtml_s751a)

We are now ready to set up our development environment. This section walks through the project’s folder organization, the required libraries, and the implementation of a **`DependenciesChecker`** class that validates our setup before development begins.

# [Project Directory Structure](#toc.xhtml_s752a)

Our approach to file organization emphasizes clarity and consistency. *[Figure 20.2](#c20.xhtml_fig20_2)* illustrates the recommended file structure for our project.

![](images/Figure-20.2.jpg)

**Figure 20.2:** TaskWise AI Application Project File Structure

Referring to *[Figure 20.2](#c20.xhtml_fig20_2)*, we see that the **`src/`** folder and its subfolders are for the Java source files. The **`lib/`** folder will hold our external libraries (JAR files). Our application will also have a **`resources/`** folder and a **`logs/`** folder.

# [Library Setup](#toc.xhtml_s753a)

Our TaskWise AI application will require three third-party libraries: one for database support; another for our AI functionality; and a third for our Graphical User Interface (GUI).

SQLite

First, we require the SQLite JDBC driver from *[Chapter 11, Database Connectivity with JDBC](#c11.xhtml)*. Alternatively, you can download the latest sqlite-jdbc JAR from this GitHub page:

**`https://github.com/xerial/sqlite-jdbc`**

Once you have the JAR file, place it in your project’s **`lib/`** folder.

**Weka**

Next, locate the Weka JAR file that you used in *[Chapter 19, Using AI with Java Programming](#c19.xhtml)* and place it in your project’s **`lib/`** folder. Alternatively, you can obtain the JAR file from this page:

**`https://www.cs.waikato.ac.nz/ml/weka/`**

As we covered in the previous chapter, Weka is a machine learning library written in Java. We are including it in our project to demonstrate how AI components can be integrated into desktop applications. TaskWise AI will make minimal use of Weka such as keyword classification or dummy model invocation.

**JavaFX**

Our third tool is JavaFX, which we will use to render our GUI and manage the UI components. Obtain the latest JavaFX SDK from the following link:

**`https://gluonhq.com/products/javafx/`**

Download the SDK specific to your operating system and CPU architecture. After you download the SDK, extract the zip/archive file and place the contents in a location you can remember. There is no installation process, you merely need to copy the contents of the JavaFX SDK’s lib folder to your project’s **`lib/`** folder.

If you have not yet installed the JavaFX Support extension in Visual Studio Code, you should do that now.

In your project’s .vscode folder, create a settings.json file with the content shown below. Be sure to use the JavaFX SDK version number that matches what you downloaded.

`{`

`"java.project.referencedLibraries": [`

`"lib/**/*.jar",`

`"/Users/yourname/javafx-sdk-24/lib/**/*.jar"`

`]`

`}`

# [Setup Verification](#toc.xhtml_s754a)

Before beginning implementation, we should verify that all required libraries are available to our application. To do this, we will create a utility class called **`DependenciesChecker`** that prints the status of each external dependency. Here is that code.

`package utils;`

`public class DependenciesChecker {`

`public static void main(String[] args) {`

`checkSQLite();`

`checkWeka();`

`checkJavaFX();`

`}`

`private static void checkSQLite() {`

`try {`

`Class.forName("org.sqlite.JDBC");`

`System.out.println("[`**`✓`**`] SQLite JDBC Driver is available.");`

`} catch (ClassNotFoundException e) {`

`System.err.println("[`**`✗`**`] SQLite JDBC Driver not found.");`

`}`

`}`

`private static void checkWeka() {`

`try {`

`Class.forName("weka.core.Instances");`

`System.out.println("[`**`✓`**`] Weka Library is available.");`

`} catch (ClassNotFoundException e) {`

`System.err.println("[`**`✗`**`] Weka Library not found.");`

`}`

`}`

`private static void checkJavaFX() {`

`try {`

`Class.forName("javafx.application.Application");`

`System.out.println("[`**`✓`**`] JavaFX is available.");`

`} catch (ClassNotFoundException e) {`

`System.err.println("[`**`✗`**`] JavaFX is not available.");`

`}`

`}`

`}`

When we run this program, it will check for the presence of our libraries and print the results to the console. Running this before we go any further will help us avoid surprises during development.

Use the command below to compile our application:

`javac --module-path lib --add-modules javafx.controls -cp “lib/sqlite-jdbc-3.47.2.0.jar:lib/weka.jar” -d bin src/utils/DependenciesChecker.java`

To run:

`java --module-path lib --add-modules javafx.controls -cp "bin:lib/sqlite-jdbc-3.47.2.0.jar:lib/weka.jar" utils.DependenciesChecker`

The output of this program should be as shown below:

`[`**`✓`**`] SQLite JDBC Driver is available.`

`[`**`✓`**`] Weka Library is available.`

`[`**`✓`**`] JavaFX is available.`

Once our dependencies are verified and the project is structured, we are ready to begin implementing TaskWise AI’s core functionality.

# [Core Functionality](#toc.xhtml_s755a)

So far, we finalized our application’s design and requirements, created the project’s file structure, and verified our dependencies. We are now ready to create TaskWise AI’s core functionality. This section walks through the core implementation of the application, broken down into logical components. We will define our core data model, then develop the user interface, integrate the SQLite database, embed the AI module, and implement exception handling and logging.

# [Creating and Managing Tasks](#toc.xhtml_s756a)

The **`Task`** class is the foundational model of our application. Each task includes the following fields ID, title, description, due date, status, and priority. Here is that class:

`package main;`

`import java.time.LocalDate;`

`public class Task {`

`private int id;`

`private String title;`

`private String description;`

`private LocalDate dueDate;`

`private String status;`

`private String priority;`

`// No-argument constructor (required for some frameworks)`

`public Task() {`

`}`

`// Full-argument constructor`

`public Task(int id, String title, String description, LocalDate dueDate, String status, String priority) {`

`this.id = id;`

`this.title = title;`

`this.description = description;`

`this.dueDate = dueDate;`

`this.status = status;`

`this.priority = priority;`

`}`

`// Getters and Setters`

`public int getId() {`

`return id;`

`}`

`public void setId(int id) {`

`this.id = id;`

`}`

`public String getTitle() {`

`return title;`

`}`

`public void setTitle(String title) {`

`this.title = title;`

`}`

`public String getDescription() {`

`return description;`

`}`

`public void setDescription(String description) {`

`this.description = description;`

`}`

`public LocalDate getDueDate() {`

`return dueDate;`

`}`

`public void setDueDate(LocalDate dueDate) {`

`this.dueDate = dueDate;`

`}`

`public String getStatus() {`

`return status;`

`}`

`public void setStatus(String status) {`

`this.status = status;`

`}`

`public String getPriority() {`

`return priority;`

`}`

`public void setPriority(String priority) {`

`this.priority = priority;`

`}`

`// toString method (optional but helpful)`

`@Override`

`public String toString() {`

`return "Task{" +`

`"id=" + id +`

`", title='" + title + '\'' +`

`", description='" + description + '\'' +`

`", dueDate=" + dueDate +`

`", status='" + status + '\'' +`

`", priority='" + priority + '\'' +`

`'}';`

`}`

`}`

Next, we will create the **`TaskManager`** class to manage the tasks in an **`ArrayList`**. Here is that code:

`package main;`

`import java.util.ArrayList;`

`import java.util.List;`

`public class TaskManager {`

`private List<Task> tasks = new ArrayList<>();`

`public void addTask(Task task) {`

`tasks.add(task);`

`}`

`public void removeTask(Task task) {`

`tasks.remove(task);`

`}`

`public List<Task> getAllTasks() {`

`return tasks;`

`}`

`public void clearTasks() {`

`tasks.clear();`

`}`

`}`

Next, we need to create our **`MainApp`** class. This is where we will create our GUI. Here is that code:

`package main;`

`import javafx.application.Application;`

`import javafx.scene.Scene;`

`import javafx.scene.control.*;`

`import javafx.scene.layout.*;`

`import javafx.stage.Stage;`

`public class MainApp extends Application {`

`@Override`

`public void start(Stage primaryStage) {`

`Label titleLabel = new Label("Title:");`

`TextField titleField = new TextField();`

`Label descLabel = new Label("Description:");`

`TextArea descArea = new TextArea();`

`Button suggestButton = new Button("Run AI Suggestion");`

`suggestButton.setOnAction(e -> {`

`String suggestion = AIAnalyzer.suggestPriority(descArea.getText());`

`Alert alert = new Alert(Alert.AlertType.INFORMATION, "Suggested Priority: " + suggestion);`

`alert.showAndWait();`

`});`

`VBox form = new VBox(10, titleLabel, titleField, descLabel, descArea, suggestButton);`

`form.setPadding(new javafx.geometry.Insets(10));`

`Scene scene = new Scene(form, 400, 300);`

`primaryStage.setTitle("TaskWise AI");`

`primaryStage.setScene(scene);`

`primaryStage.show();`

`}`

`public static void main(String[] args) {`

`launch(args);`

`}`

`}`

The next class is **`DatabaseHelper`** which, as you can tell from its name, will encapsulate all our SQLite operations. We will use JDBC to connect to the local database and run operations on it. Here is that code:

`package main;`

`import java.sql.*;`

`public class DatabaseHelper {`

`private static final String DB_URL = "jdbc:sqlite:resources/tasks.db";`

`public static void initializeDatabase() {`

`try (Connection conn = DriverManager.getConnection(DB_URL);`

`Statement stmt = conn.createStatement()) {`

`String sql = "CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS tasks (" +`

`"id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT," +`

`"title TEXT NOT NULL," +`

`"description TEXT," +`

`"dueDate TEXT," +`

`"status TEXT," +`

`"priority TEXT)";`

`stmt.executeUpdate(sql);`

`System.out.println("[`**`✓`**`] Database initialized.");`

`} catch (SQLException e) {`

`e.printStackTrace();`

`}`

`}`

`// Add methods for insertTask(), getTasks(), updateTask(), deleteTask()…`

`}`

Our next class is **`AIAnalyzer`** which we will use to implement a simple AI component that uses keyword detection to classify priority levels. This class demonstrates natural language processing and could easily be extended with Weka or a machine learning module. Here is that code:

`package main;`

`public class AIAnalyzer {`

`public static String suggestPriority(String description) {`

`if (description == null) return "Low";`

`String lower = description.toLowerCase();`

`if (lower.contains("urgent") || lower.contains("asap") || lower.contains("deadline")) {`

`return "High";`

`} else if (lower.contains("soon") || lower.contains("important")) {`

`return "Medium";`

`}`

`return "Low";`

`}`

`}`

Our last class is **`Logger`**, which we will use to handle exceptions and log events. Here is that code:

`package utils;`

`import java.io.FileWriter;`

`import java.io.IOException;`

`import java.time.LocalDateTime;`

`public class Logger {`

`private static final String LOG_FILE = "logs/app.log";`

`public static void log(String message) {`

`try (FileWriter writer = new FileWriter(LOG_FILE, true)) {`

`writer.write(LocalDateTime.now() + " - " + message + "\n");`

`} catch (IOException e) {`

`System.err.println("Could not write to log file.");`

`}`

`}`

`}`

`javac --module-path lib --add-modules javafx.controls -cp "lib/sqlite-jdbc-3.47.2.0.jar:lib/weka.jar" -d bin src/main/*.java`

To run the application, use the following command:

`java --module-path lib --add-modules javafx.controls -cp "bin:lib/sqlite-jdbc-3.47.2.0.jar:lib/weka.jar" main.MainApp`

# [Polishing and Enhancing the App](#toc.xhtml_s757a)

Now that the core features of TaskWise AI are working, it is time to polish the application and make it more powerful, user-friendly, and complete. This section suggests essential features, such as database persistence and logging, ensure tasks are retained between sessions, and enhance the user interface for a better experience. While not fully implemented here, these enhancements are excellent opportunities for independent exploration and practice.

**Enhancement 1:** Implement database persistence

**Description:** Currently, tasks exist only in memory for the duration of a session. To make the application truly useful, implement full database persistence using the **`DatabaseHelper`** class introduced earlier. You can add methods to insert, update, delete, and retrieve tasks using standard JDBC operations. Persisting tasks to an SQLite database ensures they are saved between sessions.

**Enhancement 2:** Load saved tasks on launch

**Description:** To provide continuity, retrieve all saved tasks when the application launches and populate the in-memory task list and task table (once implemented). This loading process can be performed during the **`start()`** method of your JavaFX application. Proper error handling and logging are important here to handle any issues with database connectivity.

**Enhancement 3:** Enable full CRUD functionality

**Description:** Give users the ability to perform complete Create, Read, Update, and Delete (CRUD) operations directly from the user interface. You can extend the form to support editing an existing task, and display tasks using a **`TableView`** that supports selection-based actions. Delete functionality can be added using dedicated buttons.

**Enhancement 4:** Implement logging for database operations

**Description:** Logging is essential for debugging and maintaining your application. Enhance your Logger class to capture all major operations, such as inserting or deleting a task, loading from the database, and handling exceptions. Use consistent and meaningful log messages to help you track the app’s behavior during runtime.

**Enhancement 5:** Enhance the GUI

**Description:** A polished interface improves usability and encourages continued use. Consider these enhancements:

*   Show tasks in a scrollable table (**`TableView`**) with sortable columns.
*   Use a layout manager to ensure the layout is professional.
*   Add buttons or menu items for updating and removing tasks.
*   Implement a search bar or filter to help users find specific tasks.
*   Use a CSS file to apply consistent styling or introduce a dark mode toggle for better visual comfort.
*   Add a custom TaskWise AI logo.

These enhancements will make TaskWise AI feel more complete and give you a path forward if you want to continue evolving the project.

# [Final Review](#toc.xhtml_s758a)

Once you complete your application’s enhancements, consider testing and review as part of your development workflow. Testing can help ensure that the application behaves as expected, handles errors gracefully, and meets user needs. This section outlines key strategies for evaluating TaskWise AI and preparing it for real-world use.

*   Start by manually walking through each feature of the application:
    *   Add tasks with various inputs, including empty fields or unusually long text.
    *   Trigger the AI suggestion functionality and verify that the results align with your expectations.
    *   Interact with the GUI, checking that all buttons and input fields respond properly.
    *   Restart the app to verify that saved tasks persist and load correctly.
*   Verify that all exceptions are handled cleanly. Instead of crashing, the application should display user-friendly messages and log errors for debugging. Test situations such as:
    *   Attempting to add a task without a title.
    *   Losing access to the database file.
    *   Running the app in an environment with missing dependencies.
*   Ensure that the task data remains consistent throughout the application:
    *   Updating a task in the interface should also update the stored data.
    *   Deleting a task should remove it from memory and the database.
    *   Priority levels should match the AI’s logic every time the suggestion feature is used.
*   Take time to reflect on your code organization:
    *   Are classes well-named and responsibilities clearly separated?
    *   Could any methods be refactored for readability or reuse?
    *   Have you used object-oriented principles effectively?
    *   Does your IDE display any warnings?

# [Industry Certifications](#toc.xhtml_s760a)

Industry-recognized certifications can provide evidence of your technical skills. In some cases, these certifications can even be used for credit towards a university degree. These certifications can be especially valuable when looking for jobs. Certification offers several benefits including the following:

*   Establish credibility
*   Many job listings require or prefer certifications
*   Studying for an exam reinforces key concepts and can identify areas for you to shore up
*   Confidence booster

There are two primary certifying bodies: Oracle and BlueCert.

Oracle, Java’s owner, has two primary certifications:

*   Oracle Certified Associate (OCA)
*   Oracle Certified Professional (OCP)

BlueCert is a relatively new, and robust certification platform. Their focus is on AI-adjacent technical skills, including Java development. Each of their certifications is offered in three levels (Practitioner, Associate, and Professional), each aligning with real-world roles.

# [Conclusion](#toc.xhtml_s761a)

This chapter was designed to help you further your knowledge of Java programming. By designing and implementing TaskWise AI, you put theory into practice, applied object-oriented principles, worked with JavaFX for GUI development, implemented data persistence with SQLite, and integrated a basic AI module. You also explored how to structure a project, manage dependencies, and test and refine your code.

Building a complete application from scratch can be challenging, but it offers an invaluable opportunity to consolidate and enhance your skills. You saw firsthand how individual Java concepts come together to form a functional, user-centered desktop application.

As you continue learning Java, remember that real-world development is iterative. Every enhancement you explore brings you closer to professional-grade software development.

You should now have the tools, mindset, and experience to move from beginner to practitioner. Happy programming!
